TITLE: Non-stop rocket barrage on Israel: Woman killed, terrorist infiltration from Gaza, strike on Tel Aviv
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-07T06:45:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-07/ty-article/rocket-sirens-sound-in-central-and-southern-israel/0000018b-0833-d8fc-adff-697fc62c0000

Rocket sirens were activated across central and southern Israel, and the Israeli army reported a terrorist infiltration from Gaza, in the early hours of Saturday morning.
A person was wounded in Kfar Aviv when their vehicle was hit, and a building in southern Ashkelon was damaged.
A woman was critically wounded by a rocket attack on southern Israel, and later died. Three people were also wounded in the central Israeli city of Ramle, one lightly and two seriously.
Additionally, a building in Tel Aviv sustained damage from rocket shrapnel. Israeli police reported that power lines were on the ground and warned residents to stay away remain indoors.
Residents near the Gaza border reported shooting toward their houses, and the Israeli army issued an announcement later in the day asking Israeli residents in Gaza border communities to remain inside due to a suspected terrorist infiltration.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was briefed on the incident and will convene with senior security establishment officials, according to a statement from his office.
The Education Ministry in Gaza also announced the cancellation of all school classes across Gaza for Saturday.
In September, Palestinians in Gaza protested along the border fence to two weeks in response to Jews entering the Temple Mount/Al Aqsa compound, and amid routine closures on the Erez crossing during the Jewish holidays. They announced a freeze to these protests last Thursday.
According to the announcement by the group (which calls itself "the young generation uprising"), mediators expressed intent to take steps to halt punitive measures against Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and "provocations at the Al Aqsa Mosque." Other steps included relief measures for residents of the Strip.
Last Tuesday, the Israeli army struck three Hamas position in the southern Gaza Strip. According to the IDF spokesperson, the strikes were carried out by drone, attack helicopter and tank in the Rafah crossing, Karni crossing, and Rafah crossing respectively. The IDF said that Palestinians were protesting violently in these areas, which included shooting at Israeli forces.
This is a developing story.

TITLE: Surprise infiltration, massive barrages shock Israel; Over 250 Israelis killed, 1,590 wounded; Civilians and
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-07T08:21:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-07/ty-article-live/israel-under-attack-terrorists-infiltrate-from-gaza-amid-massive-rocket-barrages/0000018b-088b-dae9-adcb-abbff50f0000

Updates
FAA advises pilots to exercise 'extreme caution' when flying over Israeli airspace
The Federal Aviation Administration advised U.S. pilots to exercise "extreme caution" when flying over Israeli airspace amid the dramatic escalation in violence between Hamas and Israel.
The warning, delivered via a Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM), described the situation as "potentially hazardous" and called on flights to maintain contact with air traffic control at all times while in the flight information region.
The FAA added that pilots should monitor NOTAMs for future possible airspace closure announcements.
Former House Speaker Pelosi to join memorial service in San Francisco to mourn Israeli victims
House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi will join the Bay Area's Jewish community on Sunday for a communal gathering to mourn Israeli victims of the Hamas attacks and to stand in solidarity with Israel while praying for peace.
Pelosi will be at San Francisco's Congregation Sherith Israel, alongside Israel's consul general to the Pacific Northwest, local rabbis and Jewish community leaders.
Analysis | Netanyahu’s recklessness has brought war upon Israel
First of all, it’s a disgrace; a deep shame fills our hearts with fury and our eyes with tears. It’s a personal tragedy, primarily for hundreds of families living near the Gaza border, who are experiencing a living hell. Then there are the hundreds of killed and wounded, including many children, followed by the shocking ease with which armed terrorists were simply able to roam around at their pleasure, in vehicles and on foot, entering Israel on the eve of a holiday, going into kibbutzim, moshavim and towns, and doing as they pleased there. For hours, residents had to fend for themselves against the terrorists, with no help from the army or police, who were far from the scene.
Israel was humiliated and routed on Saturday. A “small” terror organization exposed the nakedness of a regional superpower with intelligence and cyber capabilities that are among the best in the world. Even if all of the Gaza Strip is destroyed (and there is no need for this), and even if the heads of Mohammed Deif, Khaled Meshal, Yahya Sinwar, Ismail Haniyeh and their associates roll in the alleys, this will not make up for the biggest security failure since 1973. It will not sweeten the bitter taste of the debacle, and it won’t ease the shock of the number of those killed and kidnapped.
RECAP: At least 250 Israelis killed, more than 1600 wounded, dozens held hostage ■ 230 Palestinians killed in Gaza, over 1,700 wounded from Israeli strikes ■ Gunfights with terrorists in Gaza border communities as rockets batter Israel
Since 6 A.M. on Saturday thousands of rockets were launched from Gaza on cities across central and southern Israel, reaching as far as Jerusalem, while Palestinian terrorists infiltrated communities in the country's south by land, sea and air.
At least 250 Israelis were killed and over 1,600 were wounded throughout the day. On Saturday evening, the IDF spokesperson said the army had regained control of most of the Gaza border communities infiltrated by Hamas and Islamic Jihad militants. The military confirmed on Saturday afternoon that a "substantial" amount of Israeli civilians and soldiers are being held hostage in the Gaza Strip by Hamas militants.
In the southern cities of Be'eri and Ofakim, Israeli civilians were held captive by terrorists in their homes, which prompted outcry from a number of U.S. agencies and officials. Israeli forces released all hostages at these locations later in the night.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir declared a national state of emergency that went into effect in the evening, and called to recruit all police volunteers across the country.
The Israeli army has responded to the wave of attacks by striking Hamas positions in the Gaza Strip, which continued overnight. Palestinians report some 230 killed and over 1,700 wounded in Israeli airstrikes.
Israel's security cabinet convened Saturday night, reaching a number of operational decisions aimed at "destroying the military and governmental capabilities of Hamas," according to PM Netanyahu. These include halting electricity and fuel supply and the transfer of goods to the Gaza Strip.
"Israel is at war. This is not a so-called military operation," Netanyahu said on Saturday. Speaking at the security cabinet meeting, he said that Israel's first goal is "to purge the area of enemy forces that have infiltrated and restore security and peace to the towns that were attacked."
Netanyahu's Likud party later stated that the prime minister offered opposition leaders Yair Lapid and Benny Gantz to form an emergency unity government.
U.S. President Joe Biden said on Saturday that "This is not a moment for any party hostile to Israel to exploit these attacks," adding "The world is watching." Biden said that "The United States stands with the people of Israel in the face of these terrorist assaults," adding that "Israel has the right to defend itself and its people. Full stop."
Tens of thousands of Israeli army reserve personnel are also set to be mobilized, and a number of reserve troops participating in the protest movement against the Netanyahu government's judicial overhaul are returning to reserve duty in light of the incident.
Analysis | A failure of all systems with political shockwaves like ’73
Mid-day on Friday, a senior General Staff officer talked to a guest in his Tel Aviv office. A few minutes after the electronic clock in the office showed 2:00 P.M., the two of them noticed that they had missed the exact time the Yom Kippur War had broken out 50 years ago. The conversation drifted, naturally, to the lessons of 1973.
“In the occupied territories,” said the officer, “we are five minutes before an intifada.” He said this without knowing what he was prophesying. The host, like the entire IDF, was mainly concerned with what may transpire in the West Bank. But under the nose of the defense establishment, an unprecedented attack by Hamas was taking shape at the same time, along the Gaza border.

TITLE: At least 700 Israelis killed, 2,000 wounded; Over 130 civilians and soldiers held hostage in Gaza
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-08T06:09:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-08/ty-article-live/over-250-israelis-killed-1-590-wounded-civilians-and-soldiers-held-hostage-in-gaza/0000018b-0cd2-d8fc-adff-6dfe855e0000

Updates
Attempted terrorist attack in Hebron: Israeli soldiers thwart ramming attack by tractor driver
The IDF announced that a tractor driver attempted to carry out a ramming attack Monday morning at a military checkpoint between Hebron and Kiryat Arba in the West Bank.
According to the army's statement, the terrorist launched a live broadcast on social media while on his way to the area, and was shot by IDF soldiers.
IDF: Soldiers fought 70 terrorists Sunday night in Be’eri, suspected tunnel in the area
IDF forces fought against 70 terrorists around Kibbutz Be'eri, the IDF spokesman announced Monday morning, adding that they suspect that there is a tunnel in the area.
IDF reports encounters with terrorists in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and Nirim
IDF forces in Kibbutz Kfar Aza reported encounters with seven terrorists, who fled to the kibbutz fields. Another unit in Kibbutz Nirim reported identifying six terrorists near the kibbutz fence.
Iran denies its involvement in Hamas attack
Iran's mission to the United Nations said on Sunday that Tehran was not involved in the Hamas attack in Israel's south. "We emphatically stand in unflinching support of Palestine; however, we are not involved in Palestine's response, as it is taken solely by Palestine itself," Iran's U.N. mission said.
The mission also stated that the "measures taken by Palestine constitute a wholly legitimate defense against seven decades of oppressive occupation and heinous crimes committed by the illegitimate Zionist regime."
"They are attempting to justify their failure and attribute it to Iran's intelligence power and operational planning," the mission added.
'The most lethal assault against Jews since the Holocaust,' says Deborah Lipstadt
U.S. Special Antisemitism Envoy Deborah Lipstadt, among the most renowned Holocaust scholars in the world, called the Hamas attacks "the most lethal assault against Jews since the Holocaust."
Lipstadt said there is "no justification" for the "heinous, barbaric terrorism against Israeli civilians" and mass murder.
"No one has the right to tell Israel how to defend itself and prevent and deter future attacks. As [U.S. President Joe Biden] stated, “The United States stands with Israel. We will not ever fail to have their back… Israel has the right to defend itself and its people. Full stop."
At least four U.S. citizens killed, U.S. officials say
At least four U.S. citizens are believed to be among those killed in Israel during Saturday's Hamas attacks, senior U.S. officials told U.S. lawmakers during a Sunday night briefing.
According to several people familiar with the briefing, held by senior State Department and Defense officials, the total likely to rise in the coming days.
The White House confirmed "several" deaths of U.S. citizens earlier in the day, after U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said the Biden administration was working overtime to verify U.S. casualties and hostages.
Israel's Ambassador to the UN Gilad Erdan said "dozens" of American citizens were among the hostages.
IDF: Exchange of fire near Sderot in Israel's south
Forces were called to the scene near Sderot following an exchange of fire, according to the IDF spokesperson.
IDF Spokesperson: Israel's air force is attacking Hamas headquarters and other targets in Gaza
The air force is attacking Hamas targets in the Gaza Strip, according to the IDF spokesperson.
According to the announcement, a building housing Hamas operatives, and several Hamas headquarters, were attacked.
Israeli army reservists stranded abroad scramble to find flights back to join their units
With many international airlines cancelling their flights to Israel because of the security situation, Israel’s national airline, El Al, was in most cases their only option for getting back home.
Many of these reservists have therefore been mobilizing through WhatsApp groups to organize special charter flights to allow them join units that have been called up to fight in and around Gaza and provide reinforcements in other areas.
Others were hoping to find connections with El Al employees who might help them book seats on flights leaving within the next few hours.

TITLE: 'No justification for terrorism': World reacts to Hamas' deadly attack on Israel
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-08T14:19:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-08/ty-article/no-justification-for-terrorism-world-reacts-to-hamas-deadly-attack-on-israel/0000018b-0e9f-dae3-a1cb-bf9f532b0000

Hamas launched the largest attack on Israel in years on Saturday, killing at least 250 Israeli citizens and soldiers.
Here are the reactions from around the world:
UNITED STATES
"There is never any justification for terrorism. We stand in solidarity with the government and people of Israel, and extend our condolences for the Israeli lives lost in these attacks," U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said in a statement released by the State Department.

TITLE: Q&A: What should I do during a rocket strike or terrorist attack in Israel?
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-08T15:54:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-08/ty-article/q-a-what-should-i-do-during-a-rocket-strike-in-israel/0000018b-0f27-dcc2-a99b-1f37cbe80000

Where should I go during a rocket strike?
When you hear a rocket siren, the best option is to shelter in a "protected space" or "safe room." Many Israeli buildings have these rooms, which are designed to withstand missile attacks. Some buildings have one collective shelter for all tenants (a great way to meet your neighbors), and some have reinforced rooms built into individual apartments and homes.
There are also may be a public shelter, "miklat" in Hebrew, near you. Public shelters are maintained by the municipalities. Each municipality has a list or map of shelters available, with many translated into English. Here is Tel Aviv's map, for instance, and here is a list of public shelters in Jerusalem.
Tall office buildings and large public buildings will all have safe rooms.
If you don't have a protected space in your home or building and don't have a shelter nearby, the army's Home Front Command recommends sheltering in a stairwell that doesn't have any external walls, windows or openings. If the building is more than three stories, it advises going to the landing on a middle floor.
If you have no access to any of the above, the Home Front Command advises residents to pick a room with as few external walls, windows or openings as possible. It notes that you should stay far away from ceramic, porcelain and glass, which could shatter. With all their fixtures and items made of easily breakable materials, this means you shouldn't use a kitchen, bathroom or shower room as a protected space.
It's also important to walk – not run – to these protected spaces. It feels natural to hurry but people have been injured by tripping and falling on the way to shelter. The military says to stay in protected spaces for 10 minutes after the warning siren ends, to be sure the rocket volley is over.
Lastly, if there is no shelter available, the Home Front Command advises you to lay down on the ground on your stomach, with your arms covering your head. If you're in a vehicle, stop on the shoulder and exit the vehicle. On a train, bend down to be below the windows.
How do I know when to get to safety?
Israeli cities and towns are outfitted with siren systems, which will sound upon missile launches towards them. The advance warning depends on the distance between the missile launch point and the town in question, but may be a minute and a half at most.
Missile alert sirens are less shrill than police or ambulance sirens, and rise and fall. If you hear the siren, it's time to get to safety.
The IDF's Home Front Command also has an app, which is available for iOS and Android devices – you can download it through the unit's website here. It uses your location to send you alerts about incoming rockets. There are also other apps providing location-based missile alert service.
Can I leave the country?
Foreign carriers may halt service to war zones. As of Sunday, many airlines had halted flights in and out of Israel, including Delta, United, Virgin, EasyJet, Swiss Air, Lufthansa, Ryanair, Wizzair, Aegean, Iberia and Georgian. If you had a scheduled flight that was canceled, many of the airlines are operating helplines for customers.
As of writing Ben-Gurion International Airport was crowded, and El-Al and Arkia flights in and out of Israel may be fully booked for the coming days as tourists try to leave and Israelis try to return.
Several airlines have delayed their flights on Sunday and others have tentatively kept to schedule. Anyone with a flight booked, or hoping to catch one at the airport, should keep an eye on the flight board at Ben-Gurion.
Someone I love is missing. What can I do?
The Home Front Command and Israel Police are operating a war room to help locate missing persons. They are calling on family members of missing people to come to the center at Hanegev 4, in Airport City (Lahav 433 Unit building) with pictures of the person, information that can identify them and an item from which they can take a DNA sample.
Family members in combat areas who can't reach the building can call the police helpline at 105.
U.S. citizens seeking to be in touch with the U.S. Embassy in Israel may follow the link provided here for a crisis intake form, or call 1-833-890-9595 (toll free) and 606-641-0131 (in the U.S.). The latest security alert regarding Israel, is available here.
What if I need to talk to someone?
There are several free mental health helplines in Israel, many of which do provide English language services.
ERAN, an emotional first aid service, offers assistance via phone, online and on WhatsApp. You can reach them by dialing 1201, and the English language line by pressing 3. You can also text them at 052-999-3544, or send them a WhatsApp by clicking here.
NATAL, a nonprofit for people coping with war- and terror-related trauma, has English speaking staff on hand as well. You can reach them by phone at 1-800-363-363, and pressing 1.
If you're registered with an Israeli health maintenance organization, all of them are currently running mental health helplines.

TITLE: 'It's unthinkable. Hundreds of bereaved families, hundreds of hostages'
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-08T19:33:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/podcasts/2023-10-08/ty-article-podcast/its-unthinkable-hundreds-of-bereaved-families-hundreds-of-hostages/0000018b-0f94-dcc2-a99b-1f95030a0000

Israel's reality transformed overnight this weekend and what looks like a major war is unfolding. Events are progressing rapidly, so in this week's Haaretz podcast, editor in chief of Haaretz, Aluf Benn, and Haaretz senior analyst Yossi Melman explain in conversation with Allison Kaplan Sommer how a country that has prided itself with having the best intelligence in the world was hit hard by an unprecedented surprise attack from the Gaza Strip.
Benn says the Hamas orchestrated attack – that has already claimed the lives of over 600 Israelis - was a "total surprise," and that "there was no intelligence indicating anything remotely like this."
Even though there was a sense that Israel's enemies would take advantage of its inner rifts, "none of the warnings included anything similar to what happened yesterday."
According to Benn, "This is the worst blow to Israel in any war, since 1948, and of any terrorist attacks inside Israel or abroad. In 1973 Israel was taken by surprise, but the fighting took place far away from civilians. Now this is first and foremost an attack against civilians, and for the first time we have dozens of military prisoners of war and civilians taken hostage in Gaza. People are desperately trying to find out what happened to their family members. We know people, friends, that have children who are missing or dead. It's a very sad, unprecedented situation for all of us."
Melman addresses the "huge failure" of Israel's Intelligence. "When you talk to people in the intelligence community, they are confused, they are puzzled, they don't know what happened. They have no explanation," he says. "Certainly it was a huge failure, Israel has been prided with having the best intelligence in the world, and the intelligence failed. For many Israelis, what happened on Saturday, 50 years and one day after the Yom Kippur War started, is reminiscent of the same failure. But there is a big difference: Before the war in 1973, the intelligence was there. Israel had a lot of pieces of intelligence but didn't know how to read it or didn't want to analyze it in the correct way. This time there was nothing."
The Gaza Strip is an area Israel was supposedly watching very closely, so having hundreds of militants cross into Israel on a holiday morning was unimaginable. "It's a failure of the military intelligence, it's a failure of the domestic security service - the Shin Bet – both the organizations have the technological means to listen to the other side, to recruit agents for human intelligence. It's a huge machine of intelligence gathering that didn't function."
Looking forward, both Benn and Melman think the wounds will take years to heal. "It's going to take time for the public to realize what happened," Benn says. "We are talking about hundreds of bereaved families, hundreds of hostage families, it's still unthinkable. I'm hearing horrible stories from people I know."

WASHINGTON - The Biden administration still has every intention to pursue normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia despite the Hamas attacks, though acknowledged it is not the current main area of focus.
"We still believe that normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia is not only good for the people of those two nations, but for the American people and for everybody else in the region, and we have every intention to continue to encourage a process where normalization can occur," National Security Council spokesperson John Kirby said.
"I couldn't speculate now as to what impact the events of the last 36 hours is going to have on those efforts, but nothing's changed about our continued desire to pursue that kind of an outcome," he continued, noting that "even before the attacks of the weekend, we were months away from getting close to some sort of agreed-to negotiation."
Kirby further noted "it's too soon to say that we've hit the brakes on this. It just understandably, isn't the main area of focus right now. But I wouldn't go so far as to say we've given up on it or we don't have any interest in pursuing it."
Hamas attacks are fifth-deadliest in the world since 1970
The Hamas attacks in Israel are the fifth-deadliest terror attack in the world since 1970, according to the University of Maryland Global Terrorism Database.
The only more lethal attacks were September 11, ISIS attacks in Tikrit and Sinjar and Gikoro in Rwanda. The death toll for the Israeli attack, which already has 900 confirmed dead, is expected to rise, potentially putting it higher on the list.
The attack at the Re'im music festival, where 260 people were killed, is the deadliest attack in modern history when considered in terms of deaths relative to population, according to a Telegraph analysis of attacks in OECD countries.

TITLE: In first, archaeologists extract DNA of ancient Israelites
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-09T12:15:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/archaeology/2023-10-09/ty-article/in-first-archaeologists-extract-dna-of-ancient-israelites/0000018b-138a-d2fc-a59f-d39b21fd0000

For the first time, ancient DNA has been recovered from the bodies of ancient Israelites living in the First Temple period, Haaretz has learned.
This achievement, a Holy Grail in the study of lost civilizations, was enabled following the discovery near Jerusalem of a rare family tomb dating to the Iron Age.
So far the collaboration of archaeologists and geneticists has been able to extract genetic material from two individuals, producing partial information, which is a tiny sample indeed. But it promises to pave the way for further research on longstanding questions about the origins of the ancient Israelites, their links to earlier populations living in the Levant, as well as to modern-day Jewish people.
Preliminary results from the excavation and the DNA study were expected to be presented at a conference about new archaeological discoveries in Jerusalem and its environs on Wednesday, and Haaretz has obtained an advance copy of the researchers’ paper. The conference has since been delayed due to the ongoing conflict between Israel and Gaza.
This story begins in 2018, when the Theft Prevention Unit of the Israel Antiquities Authority discovered a tomb in the village of Abu Ghosh, which is right next to the biblical settlement of Kiryat Yearim, some 15 kilometers west of Jerusalem.
The tomb had been badly damaged, first by construction and then by looting, so the archaeologists conducted a hurried salvage excavation. Although only a fraction of the tomb had survived, the researchers uncovered some 150 pottery vessels, including bowls, jars and lamps, as well as the jumbled skeletal remains of at least 10 individuals, the archaeologists report.
Those interred in the tomb included six adults, three men and three women, and four children, including two babies, one infant, and an adolescent. This is consistent with the high mortality rate of children in ancient times, the researchers note.
Based on the pottery typology used in the funerary offerings it seems that the tomb was used for a prolonged period, around 750-650 B.C.E., placing it in the late Iron Age, or late First Temple period according to the biblical chronology.
The tomb is an important find in its own right, given that burials from this period are rare and tend to be from slightly later times, generally closer to the fall of Jerusalem and the First Temple to the Babylonians in 586 B.C.E., says Israel Finkelstein, an archaeologist at Tel Aviv University and the University of Haifa. Finkelstein was called in to lead the research on the tomb as he was already heading a dig at Kiryat Yearim, a settlement which is mentioned in the Bible as having housed the Ark of the Covenant before it was brought to Jerusalem.
“I suppose that we are dealing with a family tomb, likely from the elite of Kiryat Yearim, whose members were buried there over a long period of time,” Finkelstein says. “We don’t know how big it was originally, because most of it was destroyed in recent years.”
Together with Prof. David Reich, a geneticist at Harvard University, and mathematician Dr. Arie Shaus, Finkelstein embarked on a quest to extract DNA from the people interred in the Kiryat Yearim tomb.
Who is an ancient Jew?
The technique of extracting genetic material from ancient bones, teeth and other organic remains began to emerge over 20 years ago, and has since reached such sophistication that researchers are even divining (some) information on creatures that lived over a million years ago. It is rare for bones to be preserved well enough to provide any genetic material at all, yet the ability to extract and sequence genetic material from ancient remains has given researchers major insights into the origins, migrations and history of human populations, as well as prehistoric hominins, animals and plants.
But big questions remain when it comes to the genetic history of the Jewish people. Looking far into the past, inquisitive minds have long asked: Who were the ancient Hebrews, the inhabitants of the biblical Kingdoms of Judah and Israel in the Iron Age (12th-6th century B.C.E)? From which population did they descend and how were they connected to their neighbors, the Philistines, Edomites, Moabites and so on?
Looking at the present, we wonder what is the genetic link between First Temple-period Israelites and today’s Jews, and which other populations intermingled with them over millennia of exile, wanderings and persecutions. And then there is the big mystery surrounding the origin of modern Jewish groups, particularly of Europe’s Ashkenazi population, whose communities first emerged in the Rhineland at the height of the Middle Ages. What is their ancestral connection to the Israelites of yore?
By the way, these questions exist independently of the political conflict over competing claims to the Holy Land, although these issues are often coopted and distorted in the toxic debate over which modern population has the greatest link to the ancestral inhabitants of the Levant.
A bona fide Israelite bone
Over the years, scientists have found some indirect evidence pertaining to the genetic origins of the Israelites – more about this later – by looking at the DNA of modern Jews as well as Bronze Age Canaanites, who preceded the formation of the ancient Israelite identity. But direct access to ancient Israelite DNA and all the information contained therein has so far eluded researchers.
There are several reasons for this. Firstly, well-preserved DNA is harder to find in the hot Middle Eastern climes. But this technical issue was partly overcome by the 2015 discovery that the petrous bone, a part of the skull located behind the ear, contains a much higher concentration of DNA than other bones, meaning that at least some genetic material may survive in it even in warmer weather.
That game-changing revelation allowed scientists to shed light on everything from the genetic history of the earliest Neolithic farmers in Anatolia to the origins of the Philistines, the biblical enemies of the Israelites. But not much headway had been made on the ancient Hebrews.
That has been partly because of the rarity of ancient Hebrew graves and largely because in Judaism, excavating or disturbing graves is a big taboo. Particularly in Israel, human remains are not considered antiquities by law, and archaeologists who find ancient graves are often pressured by ultra-Orthodox groups to quickly rebury any bones they unearth.
At Kiryat Yearim, it was indeed the precious petrous bone that yielded genetic information about two of the individuals buried there, the researchers report. But before we look at the – very preliminary – results we have wonder whether we can be sure about the cultural identity of the tomb’s residents.
It’s true that no ancient Hebrew inscriptions were found in the burial confirming that the deceased were Israelites. However, the pottery assemblage is typical of what is found in late First Temple-period burials in Jerusalem, Finkelstein explains. Together with Kiryat Yearim’s proximity to what was then the capital of the Kingdom of Judah, this suggests that the locals can indeed be identified as ancient Hebrews, he says.
“Of course, cultural identity and genetic background are not the same,” Finkelstein adds. “Genetic background can be revealed by an ancient DNA study. Identity is about culture, geography and can change through the ages. This is also true in the present: just look at the population of modern Israel.”
There is also a question as to whether Kiryat Yearim was controlled by Judah or its larger, and often rival, northern neighbor, the Kingdom of Israel. Finkelstein’s recent excavations at the site have revealed a large artificial platform at the top of the settlement, which is typical of the northern kingdom’s urban planning. This suggests that Kiryat Yearim was initially under the control of Israel, at least until that kingdom was conquered by the Assyrians in the second half of the eighth century B.C.E.
In any case, the genetic data from Kiryat Yearim offers a first glimpse of how directly sampling remains from the First Temple period can shed light on the history of the ancient Hebrews, Israelite or Judahite.
The two sampled individuals were one male and one female. The conference paper only discusses data from the Y chromosome and mitochondrial DNA, sections of the genome that are inherited only from the father and mother respectively. Data gleaned from the rest of the genome will be provided in an upcoming scientific publication.
“This is only partial data with a more detailed paper coming in the future,” Reich says. “Sampling DNA from ancient Israelites is exciting, as it should make it possible to test how they relate genetically to previous groups, to contemporary non-Israelite groups, and to people living today.
And the Canaanites begat Abraham
The highlight of the very partial results is that the Y chromosome in the man belongs to the J2 haplogroup, a group of closely-related DNA sequences that is believed to have originated in the Caucasus or Eastern Anatolia, a vast area including modern-day eastern Turkey, northwest Iran, Armenia, Georgia, Azerbaijan and southern Russia.
This is important because, as mentioned, researchers have already mapped the DNA of ancient Canaanites, showing that they had a strong ancestral connection to modern-day Jewish and Arab populations. That research, published in Cell in 2020, also showed that the Canaanites in the Middle and Late Bronze Age (before the emergence of the Israelite identity) descended from a mix of Neolithic inhabitants of the Levant and a group that immigrated from the Caucasus or Eastern Anatolia.
This migration was already in motion in the Early Bronze Age, around 2900-2500 B.C.E., and is also visible archaeologically, with pottery from this period exhibiting strong influences from Anatolia and the Caucasus. It continued in the Middle Bronze Age, as seen in the study of ancient DNA of individuals from Megiddo and other places, and is evident in the mention in historical texts of Canaanite officials in the Late Bronze Age, with names that are not Semitic and originate in the northeastern Middle East, Finkelstein says.
While it’s too early to draw conclusions based on limited data from a single Israelite sample, it is of note that the First Temple-period individual from Kiryat Yearim still carried the same genetic variations that the Canaanites displayed centuries earlier and which they in turn had inherited from the Caucasian newcomers.
“As limited as it is, we cannot ignore this piece of evidence, that there is a connection between the genetic background of this person at Kiryat Yearim in the first millennium B.C.E. and the Canaanites in the second millennium B.C.E.,” Finkelstein says. “It’s not a complete surprise because we have evidence from other lines of inquiry, but it is another, small piece of evidence showing that the genetic pool is the same. Of course, at this time we cannot say if this is representative of the entire population.”
If researchers gather more data confirming that most Israelites indeed shared this ancestry with the Canaanites, it would support something that experts have strongly suspected for a while, that in fact the ancient Hebrews descended from the Canaanites.
The biblical stories stress a discontinuity between the Canaanites, often depicted in a negative light, and the pious Israelites, described as non-local descendants of a Mesopotamian-born patriarch, Abraham.
Out of Anatolia
Yet archaeologists have long noted that the similarities between Canaanite and Israelite material culture, language and settlement patterns all suggest that the latter simply grew out of the former.
“In the last 30-40 years there is a general understanding that the Hebrews were mostly of local origin, which means they were Canaanites and became Israelites in an identity-forming process that probably took a long time,” Finkelstein says.
This process started at the end of the Bronze Age, around the 12th century B.C.E., when the so-called Bronze Age Collapse saw the destruction of multiple civilizations across the Mediterranean and the withdrawal of Egypt from Canaan, which the pharaohs had controlled for centuries. In the ensuing power vacuum, the local Canaanites formed new cultural identities around the emerging territorial entities we are familiar with from the Bible: Moab, Edom, Aram, Ammon and of course Judah and Israel (the partial exception here being the Philistines who do appear to have received an influx of Aegean migrants).
As for the mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited from the maternal side, the two individuals at Kiryat Yearim displayed two different haplogroups. One, T1a, is a very ancient ancestral haplogroup, with similar counterparts already found in individuals living in Jordan some 10,000 years ago and in southeastern Europe around 7,000 years ago, says Shaus. In later samples it is found in Iran and in those Canaanites sampled in Israel, as well as all the way to the Baltic and Ural Mountains.
This suggests that this haplogroup’s initial source may have been somewhere in Neolithic Anatolia or the Levant, and slowly spread with early farming, Shaus says.
The second mitochondrial haplogroup, called H87, hasn’t been previously detected in ancient DNA samples but is found in modern-day Basques, Tunisian Arabs, and Iraqis. This may point to an origin in the Mediterranean or the Near East, perhaps in the Arabian peninsula, he says. If so, this particular haplogroup may have spread with nomadic populations, Shaus concludes. In other words, the samples from two ancient Israelites hint at ancestry from peoples in both Anatolia and Arabia.
Much more data and research are needed to understand how significative these results are, whether they truly represent the ancestry of the region’s population at the time – and what they mean for our understanding of the broader story of the emergence of ancient Israel.

TITLE: Bank of Israel to sell $30b of foreign currency to stabilize shekel amid Gaza war
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-09T12:44:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-09/ty-article/bank-of-israel-to-sell-30b-of-foreign-currency-to-stabilize-shekel-amid-gaza-war/0000018b-13ba-dcc2-a99b-17bbf9b40000

The Bank of Israel said on Monday it will sell up to $30 billion of foreign currency in the open market, in the central bank's first ever sale of foreign exchange, to maintain stability during Israel's war with Palestinian militants in Gaza.
The move appeared to quickly calm the market as the shekel recovered from steep early losses.
"The bank will operate in the market during the coming period in order to moderate volatility in the shekel exchange rate and to provide the necessary liquidity for the continued proper functioning of the markets," it said in a statement.
The central bank also said it would provide liquidity through SWAP mechanisms in the market of up to $15 billion.
"The Bank of Israel will continue monitoring developments, tracking all the markets, and acting with the tools available to it as necessary," it said.
Ahead of the announcement, the shekel had weakened by more than 2 percent to a more than 7-1/2 year low of 3.92 per dollar. The shekel now stands at a rate of 3.86, down 0.6 percent.
The shekel was already weak, down 10 percent versus the U.S. currency so far in 2023, largely due to the government's judicial overhaul plan that has sharply curtailed foreign investment.
Israeli stock and bond prices slid 7 percent and many businesses were closed on Sunday, a day after Hamas gunmen from Gaza killed 700 Israelis and abducted dozens more in the deadliest incursion into Israeli territory since Egypt and Syria's attacks in the Yom Kippur war 50 years ago.
Israel has amassed forex reserves of more than $200 billion, much of it from buying forex since 2008 to try and keep the shekel from strengthening too much and harm exporters as foreign inflows to the country's tech sector soared.
The last time the bank intervened was in January 2022.
Last month, Bank of Israel Governor Amir Yaron told Reuters that despite the sharply weaker shekel that has helped to push up inflation, there was no need to intervene since there were no market failures.

SOURCE: haaretz

The U.S. is discussing the creation of a humanitarian corridor for the residents of the Gaza Strip with Israel and Egypt, says Jake Sullivan, the U.S. National Security Advisor.
"I'm not going to get into the details of that about a specific crossing or so forth," said Sullivan, "only to say that that is something we are focused on and we are working on."
Sullivan added that he prefers to leave the talks to diplomatic channels, saying "When we have more to offer on that, I'll be sure that we do so."
IDF attacks 200 targets in Gaza's Al-Furqan neighborhood
Israeli fighter jets attacked about 200 targets in the Al-Furqan neighborhood in Gaza, the third attack in this area in the last day.
The IDF says the neighborhood serves as a "nest of terror."
Blinken: 'Hamas have no justification, no legitimacy, and must be universally condemned'
U.S. Secretary of State Antony J. Blinken spoke today with Israel's Strategic Affairs Minister Ron Dermer, according to the State Department spokesperson Matthew Miller.
The Secretary reiterated his profound condolences for the Hamas terrorist attack on Israel and reaffirmed unequivocal U.S. support for Israel’s right to defend itself and its citizens against this attack. The Secretary and the Minister made clear that the terrorist actions of Hamas have no justification, no legitimacy, and must be universally condemned.
U.S. President Joe Biden and Prime Minister Netanyahu provide updates in call between the two leaders

He also told Netanyahu that all countries should unequivocally condemn Hamas’s brutal atrocities, which are akin to the atrocities of ISIS from many years ago.
The two leaders agreed they will speak again in the coming days.
Parades in support of Gaza held in West Bank cities; Palestinians clashed with soldiers in Hawara
Parades in support of Gaza were held in Nablus, Ramallah and Jenin in the West Bank overnight, where a general strike has also been declared.
Clashes erupted between participants and the IDF in several locations, including in the flash point town of Hawara.

Two Palestinians have reportedly been killed in clashes with settlers and police in Silwan, according to Fatah.
Palestinian reports: IDF targets home of Hamas military leader Mohammed Deif
According to Palestinian reports, the IDF attacked the home of Hamas military commander Mohammed Deif, in Khan Younis, killing his father, brother, children and other relatives.

TITLE: France, Germany, Italy, U.K., U.S. condemn Hamas, pledge to ensure Israel's ability to defend itself
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-10T10:35:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-10/ty-article/france-germany-italy-u-k-u-s-pledge-to-ensure-israels-ability-to-defend-itself/0000018b-186f-d465-abbb-1cff64fb0000

France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, and the United States issued a joint statement on Tuesday denouncing Hamas' attack on Israel, which killed over 900 Israelis and wounded over 2,400 others, pledging to ensure Israel's ability to defend itself.
"We express our steadfast and united support to the State of Israel, and our unequivocal condemnation of Hamas and its appalling acts of terrorism," says the statement on behalf of French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak and U.S. President Joe Biden.
France, Germany, Italy, United Kingdom, and the United States — We express our steadfast and united support to the State of Israel, and our unequivocal condemnation of Hamas and its appalling acts of terrorism. Here is our joint statement.
Show more
"We make clear that the terrorist actions of Hamas have no justification, no legitimacy, and must be universally condemned," the statement continues. "In recent days, the world has watched in horror as Hamas terrorists massacred families in their homes, slaughtered over 200 young people enjoying a music festival, and kidnapped elderly women, children, and entire families, who are now being held as hostages."
The leaders further noted that "Our countries will support Israel in its efforts to defend itself and its people against such atrocities. We further emphasize that this is not a moment for any party hostile to Israel to exploit these attacks to seek advantage."
They added that "All of us recognize the legitimate aspirations of the Palestinian people, and support equal measures of justice and freedom for Israelis and Palestinians alike. But make no mistake: Hamas does not represent those aspirations, and it offers nothing for the Palestinian people other than more terror and bloodshed."
"Over the coming days, we will remain united and coordinated, together as allies, and as common friends of Israel, to ensure Israel is able to defend itself, and to ultimately set the conditions for a peaceful and integrated Middle East region," the statement concluded.

TITLE: My son has been missing since Saturday. God, please give me answers
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-10T18:14:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-10/ty-article-opinion/my-son-has-been-missing-since-saturday-god-please-give-me-answers/0000018b-1959-d2fc-a59f-d959a60c0000

I awoke to war.
I sent a WhatsApp to my son, "Speak to me." I called him. Tried not to be a nervous mother. No answer. I did it a few more times.
Hours passed. I realized that he had been at the [Supernova music festival in the Re'im Forest]. There was no longer a way to escape these feelings. I wasn't hysterical, I just wanted to know that everything was okay. I wrote a post on Facebook. Immediately there were dozens of shares and phone calls, concern from everyone around me.
And I prayed that he just had no battery on his phone. That he'd call and be mad at me, say "Why are you exaggerating Mom, all of Facebook is full of pictures of me, what's the big deal, I was at a party. Why are you so nervous?"
And I couldn't breathe anymore. They were sending me lists and I didn't see your name. I was just trying to breathe. I wanted to hear you.
What do I tell your grandparents?
I was just beginning to have bad thoughts. I was so scared. I couldn't peel my eyes from the TV, the phone. I was petrified. I just prayed that end you'd be angry at me for being worried and exaggerating the whole thing.
They all contacted their families and you didn't call me. Nu, call me.
How can I imagine a life that you're not a part of? You were supposed to visit in three days.
I got a phone call that they saw you, and I asked for a photo to believe it. It turned out to be another blond man. Again I was thrown into uncertainty. We opened a war room. We were all keeping up with reports, shares, phone calls.
Dammit Kesh, answer already.
It's not a joke anymore. Hours passed and still nothing. The post on Facebook amassed over 1,400 shares within three hours. And reports and phone calls and lots of concern and hope and prayers.
It was already 3:40 P.M. I had started searching for you at 9 A.M. They abducted civilians to Gaza, I only hoped that you weren't among them. I went through horror scenarios. What's better: Wounded? Dead? Captive? God, give me my son. Give me answers.
A phone call from a friend, who shared rumors that he was wounded. Maybe in Soroka [Medical Center]. I couldn't live with "maybe" but it's preferable to being abducted in Gaza, isn't it? And if he was seriously wounded, and he's in the hospital, and he has a few hours left, and I'm not with him? Should I travel for three hours to search in a chaotic hospital? I was at a loss, I had no idea what to do.
I've been at Soroka for two hours already, there was no information. Phone calls, prayers, and I had no idea where you were.
The trip was hard. I imagined scenarios, each more frightening than the other. We arrived at the hospital reception center. I saw a woman opposite me who I didn't know. I started to cry. "How do I start?" I asked her. I came from Eilat, so that if my son is seriously injured and has a few hours, I'll be with him. Let him just be alive please. We'll manage with the rest.
We were at the police station in Be'er Sheva. A bad movie that doesn't end. Keshet, yalla, wake up, wherever you are and call me. At any hour. I'd come running to you. I've already recited Tehilim (Psalms), would you believe? I couldn't think.
Let this horror end, be alive. Please.
I gave a DNA sample. I prayed that they'd say that you're unconscious, that until now they hadn't identified you. Back to Soroka. It was impossible to sleep. I fluctuated between hope and despair. Until there's certainty, there are no answers. God, this is your time. Help me and my family.
2:15 A.M. The hospital was already quite empty. There were 20 unidentified patients left. Helicopters and ambulances kept arriving. And kind people who set up a big table and offered food and drink that they'd brought from home. I hadn't been able to eat a crumb all day. I didn’t feel any desire to sleep – how could I? And they were still continuing to pray for you everywhere my beloved Keshet. Yalla, it's time for you to come back already.
I went on Facebook again, where your picture stared out at me from every shared post. It even reached [Israeli singer] Omer Adam, would you believe it?
I posted a small update because people hadn't stopped messaging me. This way maybe I'd get some peace and quiet.
5:10 A.M. and still nothing. My stomach churned. A soldier outside said that there were more bodies in the area, hundreds at the site of the outdoor rave. I couldn't breathe.
We returned home. We arrived at 9 A.M. We've been awake for 24 consecutive hours. And nothing. On the way I heard a guy on the radio describing the inferno and the massacre at the party. And I could no longer hold back my tears and my pain. I imagined you, what you were going through, what you went through, what your eyes saw … The dimensions of the hell I was in kept growing. I was suffocating.
I told your grandparents. It was already impossible to hide it from them. I saw their world collapse before them. People were praying for your welfare all over the world, my Keshet. All you have to do is come back with your smile.
I was able to sleep for two hours, barely. This day is going to be long.
When I got up I spoke to Elazar and Yitzhak, who were there with you. I understood that your foot was injured, apparently by a car, maybe one that was fleeing, maybe theirs. And then they told me something that I can't even utter. Or imagine. They said that you are probably in their hands, wounded or dead, God forbid.
I feel like I'm in a movie. I'm part of the cast. It's a bad, bizarre film. And I have no idea, because I haven't heard from any source, what's with my son.
8 P.M. This day isn't over. Nerve-racking waiting. How many days like this will we have? Again, rumors about a photo in which you can be seen. I absolutely refuse to pay attention to those pictures. I'll continue to wait for reliable information. But it's discouraging.
An entire day has passed. And still nothing. Bizarre things that I wouldn't have dreamed of doing: I joined a WhatsApp group for first-degree relatives of missing persons and captives. I was interviewed in the media. I said "Shin Bet" at least once every hour. And the list goes on.
Keshet, you can't imagine how many people love you. Us. On every continent, in every language, in every religion. They're praying for you to return safely and speedily.
I'm maintaining relative serenity. I'm keeping calm. But today, in the car as we drove to bring clothes to evacuees from the Gaza border communities in Eilat, they played the song "Zemer Nuge" (also known as "Hatishma Koli" ["Will you hear my voice?"]) on the radio, and I couldn't keep it in anymore. When it comes to songs, I break down. And I wanted to shout the song out loud and I couldn't utter a single word, I could only cry. "I'll wait for you until the end of my life."
The writer is the mother of Keshet Casarotti Kalfa, who has been missing since Saturday morning.

According to the announcement, the Hamas commando force ("Nohva") was one of the leaders of the raid on Israeli cities on Saturday, and the headquarters that were attacked were used by his fighters who participated in the attack.
It was also reported that in an attack in Rafah, Muhammad Abu Shamla, a senior operative from the Hamas navy, was killed. According to the IDF, Abu Shamla's house was also used to store naval weapons intended for attacks against Israel.
Strikes in Gaza overnight killed 33 people within 2 hours
IDF strikes in the Gaza Strip killed 33 people within two hours overnight on Thursday according to an Al Jazeera correspondent in Gaza.

The envoy added that since the fighting began, six neighborhoods in the Gaza Strip had been destroyed.
IDF Spokesman to International Media: Priority is given to attacking senior Hamas members

"We are trying to reach the lower layer that Hamas has built for itself," he said. Former U.S. President Donald Trump says Israel needs to 'straighten themselves out' following Hamas attack
Former U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday sharply criticized Israel for not participating in the assassination of Iranian General Qassem Soleimani, saying Israel needs to “straighten themselves out” following the Hamas attacks.
“I’ll never forget that Bibi Netanyahu let us down. That was a very terrible thing, I’ll say that. So when I see sometimes the intelligence - you talk about the intelligence, you talk about the things that went wrong over the last week - they’ve got to straighten it out, because they’re fighting potentially a very big force. They’re fighting potentially Iran, and when they have people saying the wrong things, everything’s being digested by these people because they’re vicious and they’re smart.”
“We were disappointed by that, very disappointed,” he said, referring to Netanyahu’s reaction to the Qassem Soleimani assassination.
“Bibi tried taking credit for it,” trump said laughing. “That didn’t make me feel too good.”
Biden discusses Hamas attacks with UAE President, stressing humanitarian assistance importance
U.S. President Joe Biden and UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed on Wednesday discussed the Hamas attacks on Israel, with the U.S. readout stressing "the importance of ensuring humanitarian assistance reaches those in need."
The U.S. said earlier Wednesday it was in active discussions with Israel and Egypt about creating safe passage for Palestinian civilians wishing to flee the fighting in Gaza.
The U.S. raised the travel advisory for Israel to "level 3 - reconsider travel."
"Terrorist groups, lone-actor terrorists and other violent extremists continue plotting possible attacks in Israel and the West Bank and Gaza. Terrorists and violent extremists may attack with little or no warning, targeting tourist locations, transportation hubs, markets/shopping malls, and local government facilities. Violence can occur in Israel and the West Bank and Gaza without warning. There has been a marked increase in demonstrations throughout Israel, some with little or no warning," the new guidance from the State Department reads.
The new guidance comes one day after U.S. Homeland Security Advisor Liz Sherwood-Randall said the Biden administration is working on a number of different options to ensure any U.S. citizen who wants to leave Israel can do so despite the limited capacity on commercial flights departing Ben-Gurion International Airport.

"We want to make it real clear," he said. "We're working on every aspect of the hostage crisis in Israel, including deploying experts to advise and assist with recovery efforts."
Gantz: Standing here shoulder to shoulder sends clear message to adversaries, Israeli citizens
Benny Gantz, who joined an emergency government with Netanyahu, stated on Wednesday that his cooperation with the government is "a clear message to our adversaries and to all Israeli citizens: all of us together are mobilizing." Gantz said after the Security Cabinet meeting in which he participated, "Just as people from left and right, from the city and the village, go out to fight, decisions of the government will also be made by people from different camps. Now, we are all one camp - the camp of the people of Israel."

TITLE: Five hours after gruesome attack began, a satellite captured Hamas atrocities in Israel
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-11T09:07:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/security-aviation/2023-10-11/ty-article-magazine/five-hours-after-gruesome-attack-began-a-satellite-captured-hamas-atrocities-in-israel/0000018b-1d2f-d465-abbb-1dbf49fc0000

At 11:31 Saturday morning, five hours after Hamas’ attack began, a European Space Agency satellite passed over Israel and photographed the massacre’s aftermath in communities near the Gaza Strip.
Sentinel-2 is one of two twin Earth observation satellites that continuously survey the planet, photographing each locale every five days.
Hamas’ assault took place in many locales. The satellite images show smoke and fire rising from sites where rockets and mortars landed, from combat, from kibbutz homes torched with their residents inside and from the parking lot at Kibbutz Re’im, where hundreds of Israelis were slaughtered while attending a rave.
The scene at the entrance to Sderot was unbelievable. Bodies were lined up at the city’s entrance, one after another. Rocket barrages, which continued nonstop, were just the soundtrack of the atrocity. So far, 20 people have been declared dead in Sderot – nine civilians, six police officers, three firefighters and two soldiers.
To the west, in Netiv Ha’asara, 15 people were murdered. The terrorists who invaded from Gaza held the moshav for hours.
At Kibbutz Be’eri, 108 Israelis were massacred. Hamas terrorists entered the kibbutz, shot residents, burned down houses and took many hostages. Those who were spared began arriving at a Dead Sea hotel Saturday night, after having been trapped in their homes for 12 hours or more.
During that time, Hamas terrorists shot, murdered and torched, destroying their kibbutz, their homes and their lives. When they were finally able to leave, the survivors saw complete devastation. They also discovered that many people they knew were no longer with them, and it’s not clear what became of them.
At Kfar Azza, removal of the dead began only on Tuesday. Army officers won’t say how many died, because finding them all is likely to take days. The military rabbinate’s victim identification personnel and the Home Front Command’s first responders were going house to house. “It’s at the least as terrible, and apparently even worse, than what happened at Kibbutz Be’eri,” one said quietly.
“Toward 7 A.M. on Saturday, amid the incessant explosions and sirens, a blood-chilling sound was heard on Kibbutz Nahal Oz for the first time – automatic rifle fire. First at a distance, in the fields; then closer, on the road; and then right in our neighborhood, outside our window. There was also shouting in Arabic.
We immediately understood what had happened – our worst nightmare had come true. Armed Hamas fighters had penetrated the kibbutz, and they were no on our doorstep, while we were locked inside with our daughters”. Around ten residents were killed and another ten or so were kidnapped to Gaza.
Israel’s October 7 disaster has more than one Ground Zero. But one of the most shocking is the parking lot where a rave was held near Kibbutz Re’im. It’s impossible to describe the scenes there in words. You can only list the sights that go on for a kilometer.
There are hundreds of burned and bullet-riddled cars, huge wet bloodstains buzzing with flies and emitting a sickening odor, bags with body parts collected by the ZAKA organization, thousands of bullets and casings and shrapnel of every kind. 250 Israeli bodies were removed from this hell the day before. And on top of all this are piles of personal belongings that bear witness to the party – tents, sleeping bags, knapsacks and water bottles.
Dozens are dead and missing in Kibbutz Nir Oz. Full details of the atrocities in these and many other communities will continue emerging in the coming days.

TITLE: How to talk to your children about the Israel-Gaza war
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-11T13:45:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-11/ty-article/how-to-talk-to-your-children-about-the-israel-gaza-war/0000018b-1b54-df31-a99f-7fd7f1430000

I’ve lived in this beautiful, wild, wonderful, frustrating, resilient little country for 13 years now. I married a true sabra and our three children were all born and are being raised here. I’ve mastered the language. I’ve opened and run a nonprofit organization here. But because I didn’t grow up here, the classic Israeli response when something bad happens, “yihyeh beseder” - "it will be all right" - will forever remain a foreign concept to me.
As I immersed myself in Israeli society, I began to see the other side of “hakol beseder,” everything’s fine. Anytime I was worried about anything, if I wanted to prepare in advance or ask a question or raise a concern, I was inevitably told that everything would be fine, motek, sweetie. As a planner and a worrier, I hated hearing this sentence, though it was always meant to reassure me.
Then in 2012, six weeks after my first child was born, Hamas launched a barrage of rockets into Israel, sending all of us running to shelters even as the Iron Dome anti-missile system did a magnificent job of protecting its citizens. I was a brand-new mother, I had never experienced any type of wartime attack, and my husband had been called up for reserve duty. I was, to put it mildly, freaking out. But everywhere I turned I was being told not to worry, that it would be over soon, that everything would be fine.
When I began to work in Israeli educational frameworks and also started having sabra babies of my own, I started to see what “yihyeh beseder” looks like for children. It has several variations: “hakol beseder,” everything’s fine; “lo kara klum,” nothing happened, and my personal least-favorite, “lo livkot,” don’t cry. As a fierce advocate of validating children’s feelings and helping them regulate their emotions by first acknowledging their existence, this has never sat well with me. In every context I have worked in, I have tried to move the needle just a little bit. To ask parents and teachers to think about what it really means to tell a child who is upset that everything is “fine.”
Sunday we all woke up to the realization that yesterday was not a collective nightmare that we all dreamed up together but, in fact, a horrific reality. The unspeakable acts of violence rattle around in our brains as does the uncertainty of what happens next. To be clear, our natural tendency as teachers and parents to reassure our children that everything is okay is not specific to Israel nor is it necessarily wrong. Anyone faced with a child who is scared wants first and foremost to help them feel less scared. This is one of our jobs as the adult presence in their lives.
But we have to do this while also remaining honest and authentic, and without discounting their very real fears and emotions. It’s a fine line to be sure, but one we are required to walk. Starting with our very youngest, and perhaps most vulnerable, citizens: babies and toddlers. Obviously, they won’t know the details of what is happening but if there is any extra stress or fear in their environment, they will most certainly sense these changes.
Keeping in mind how keenly aware babies are of the nonverbal cues we unwittingly give them can help us to regulate our own emotions around them. We want to try and stick as closely as possible to their routine while being available (emotionally and physically) for extra cuddles and reassurance for anyone who might need it.
When catastrophic events are taking place in the world, even young children are most likely hearing snippets of very scary things. While we are all doing our best to shield our children from the horrifically gruesome images on the news and the internet, we need to understand that even very young children are keenly aware of what is happening all around them.
The first and trickiest step when talking to children about the security situation is to figure out where they are at without peppering them with too many questions or, worse, instilling a fear in them that was never there to begin with. If your child doesn’t specifically vocalize their feelings, look out for changes in behavior that might indicate worry or anxiety: Loss of appetite, sleep disruption, bed-wetting or suddenly not wanting to go to school or preschool can be clues that something is wrong. A simple “How are you?” or “How are you feeling?” might be enough to open up a discussion. Children who aren’t ready for a sit-down conversation can be encouraged to express themselves through drawing or play or movement.
For children who are talking or asking questions about the attacks, here are a few guidelines for walking that line between reassurance and fearmongering.
Take a step back
Sometimes our children’s questions catch us off-guard, but as much as possible try to prepare for these types of conversations by first processing your own feelings. Perhaps this is the time to step out of our default “hakol beseder” mentality. Maybe the security situation is scarier now that we are parents. Maybe it’s hard to keep our child calm when we aren’t feeling calm ourselves. We may be carrying around related traumas from our past that we have not confronted. Our own feelings will influence the way we talk to our children about what is happening.
Be honest without oversharing
For children who have even an inkling of the violent events of the past few days, it is important to provide them with the basic facts and acknowledge that these are terrible and frightening stories. But remind them that they are also incredibly rare, even if it doesn’t feel that way because everyone is talking about them so much right now.
Talk honestly about your own feelings
One way to validate what your child is going through is to reassure them that they are not alone in their feelings. Obviously this doesn’t mean stoking their fears by telling them just how scared you are. But you can say something like “When these acts of violence happen, they don’t always make sense to us. Sometimes even grown-ups can have trouble dealing with their feelings.” Temper this with lots of reassurance that no matter what, the adults in their life are there to help them if they are feeling scared and to keep them safe.
Review safety protocols
Even as we try to keep our children in as regular a routine as possible, the current security situation demands that we follow certain directives and protocols, all of which are changing by the day. Go over any changes you are making to your regular routine and whatever procedures are recommended in your area. Talking about this with your child isn’t just best practice from a safety perspective, it can also reassure them by giving them proactive steps they can take to keep themselves safe.
Older children can even be involved in a discussion on what these changes will be. During the last round of rocket attacks my then 8-year-old at one point refused to leave the shelter in our building. We had a long conversation in which we validated her fears while also trying to get to the bottom of what she was really afraid of. It turned out she was terrified of hearing an air-raid siren and not being able to get to a shelter. We came to an agreement that for now we wouldn’t go anywhere that wasn’t within a short distance of a shelter, which meant no car rides or long walks. We showed her which buildings on our street were keeping their doors unlocked and we checked to make sure the public shelter in the neighborhood park was open.
These precautions enabled her to leave our shelter and spend some time in the fresh air. Of course, ultimately my husband and I have final say in any decision that affects our children’s well-being. But including her in the process gave her a sense of ownership and control over her personal safety.
The bigger picture
Aside from safety concerns, older children are likely to ask who is perpetrating these attacks and why. You know your child best and how much information they can process. No matter how much or little you choose to share, putting these attacks within their larger context will help children make sense of what is happening. And never be afraid to say “I don’t know.” Part of keeping the dialogue going is acknowledging that as a parent you do not have all the answers.
Despite everything I have said, I can still appreciate the broader concept of “yihyeh beseder.” While it might not be an appropriate response to a child who is feeling scared, I do think there is beauty to be found in its ultimate message of hope and optimism. But there are times when we need a more nuanced approach. Instead of “hakol beseder,” try, “There are sad and scary things happening right now and it’s okay to be feeling nervous or angry or even confused. I feel that way too. But I am here with you and I will keep you safe. And yes, everything will be okay.”

U.S. lawmaker: White House says Israel will not cut civilians in Gaza off from food, water and medicine

U.S. lawmakers call for Washington to also evacuate Palestinian-Americans in Gaza, West Bank
WASHINGTON - 17 U.S. lawmakers urged the State Department to expand its guidance on evacuating U.S. citizens from Israel to include Palestinian-Americans and U.S. citizens in Gaza and the West Bank.
The State Department earlier Thursday announced that it would begin organizing charter flights for those in Israel starting tomorrow, but did not issue any information for Palestinians.
"We write to express our concern about the lack of clear information available to our constituents who are trying to leave Gaza and the West Bank," wrote the lawmakers, led by Rep. Sara Jacobs (the youngest Jewish Democrat in Congress).
The lawmakers further requested the State Department ensure embassy staff fluent in Arabic are available to assist, and publicize the information in an accessible manner.

The National Emergency Management Authority at Israel's Defense Ministry announced the launch of a new initiative that will allow residents of Sderot to go out to rejuvenate themselves in guest houses subsidized by the state. TITLE: Israel's government 'will be held accountable' for Hamas attack, education minister says
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-12T18:04:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-12/ty-article/israels-government-will-be-held-accountable-for-hamas-attack-education-minister-says/0000018b-2407-dd34-afdf-f587246d0000

Israeli Education Minister Yoav Kisch became the first member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s cabinet to publicly take responsibility for the miscalculations that led to the deadly Hamas surprise ambush.
"This happened under our government, conclusions will be drawn, and we will be held accountable," Kisch said in an interview Thursday, following six days in which senior coalition members avoided public appearances, and those who stood before the cameras declined to address the issue of accountability for mistakes.
Speaking to Israeli news site Ynet, he said the events leading up to Saturday’s attack and how the attack unfolded “must be examined” vowing that scrutiny “will happen from all directions. Kisch called the war “a terrible disaster,” adding that Israelis must “gather our strength, fight and win,” asking “every Zionist party” to join the emergency government established on Wednesday by Netanyahu and National Unity Party leader Benny Gantz.

Echoing other government leaders’ declarations of an intent to destroy Hamas as a military and political force, Kisch recounted a meeting with a mother from southern Israel who had successfully protected herself and her children from the terrorist incursion.
“She looked me in the eyes and said to me, 'Promise me that what is happening in Gaza, that this Hamas in Gaza, will not happen again.’ I looked her in the eyes and said to her 'There will be no Hamas in Gaza, period.'"
Making sure that "there will be no Hamas left, period” said Kisch, “is our mission - and we are determined to carry it out. The IDF has everyone’s backing, even after the surprise and failure of Saturday morning. The IDF has strong capabilities, and we will win."
