TITLE: Australian Jewish community's interfaith relations strained since Gaza War
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-17T15:44:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-17/ty-article/australian-jewish-communitys-interfaith-relations-strained-since-gaza-war/0000018b-3d14-d101-a9ab-bf3cff230000

The failure of other faith communities to condemn Hamas’s massacre of 1,300 Israelis a week ago Saturday has devastated members of the Australian Jewish community who have worked closely with their Muslim and Christian counterparts for years.
No Muslim organization or cleric has spoken out against the massacre of Israeli civilians on October 7, and Christian organizations have also been largely silent.
“We are learning very quickly who our friends are at this difficult time,” said Daniel Aghion, the president of the Melbourne-based Jewish Community Council of the state of Victoria. “We have had messages of support from the Hindu community, the Buddhists, the Assyrians and the Iranian Australians. The Ethnic Community Council of Victoria has also been supportive. Unfortunately, with a few other exceptions, that is the total amount of faith and ethnic support we have received.
“As a result, the [Jewish Community Council of Victoria] is considering its position in respect to a number of bodies and whether to continue our involvement with them.”
The Jewish Christian Muslim Association and Faith Community Council of Victoria have both failed to condemn the massacres. The president of the Jewish Christian Muslim Association, Rabbi Gabi Kaltmann, has resigned, and past president Rabbi Ralph Genende intends to do so this week, saying the only reason he has not done so sooner is that he was too angry to write a considered resignation letter.
“I’m so disillusioned with all the years that I have put into interfaith work since 2011,” he said. “If they can’t see the difference between Hamas and Islamic ideology, then who are we dealing with?” he said.
“I wish they could find the moral clarity to differentiate between the genuine desire of Palestinians for recognition and the deep seated and twisted desire to rid Israel of all Jews from the river to the sea.”
Plus61J Media understands that the Islamic Council of Victoria has blocked multicultural and interfaith groups from expressing sympathy with Israel. A minority of Muslims have blatantly celebrated the murders, notably at a mosque in the Sydney suburb of Lakemba last week.
The Hamas attacks on a string of Israeli border communities were carried out at the same time as Hamas launched massive rocket barrages at Israeli towns and cities in the south and center of the country. Israel has responded with intensive aerial bombing of targets in the Gaza Strip.
Thousands of Muslims and other Australians have reacted to the events by demonstrating in support of the Palestinian cause. The Muslim community has consistently characterized Hamas as liberation fighters justified in their murder of Israeli civilians.
Last week, the Australian National Imams Council urged all imams, khateebs (preachers) and community leaders to dedicate their Friday sermons to the topic “In support of Palestine.” Their recommendations for sermons contained no mention of the atrocities of October 7 and instead urged Muslims to pray for “the innocent Palestinian victims and souls lost in recent attacks”.
The imams asked Muslims to distinguish between political Zionism and Judaism and the Jewish people and urged their community “not to condone any activity that spreads hatred and division among the people of Australia”.
A coalition of 41 Australian Islamic organizations issued a four-page statement in support of Palestine which did not mention the murder or kidnapping of Israeli civilians and claimed that the statement that “Israel has a right to defend itself” is “an egregious denial of justice and fairness to Palestinians”.
At a pro-Palestinian rally on Sunday that drew a crowd of more than 10,000, Islamic Council of Victoria President Adel Salman praised Palestinian fighters. “My heart swells with pride for the amazingly brave and courageous Palestinian people who are protesting, risking their lives, fighting against the worst form of oppression.”
The lack of support for the Jewish community, many of whom have friends and relatives affected by the attacks, has fed into the fear that is pervading the Jewish community.
To the rabbis and other Jewish leaders who have worked on interfaith relations for many years, the failure of colleagues to speak out against atrocities committed on Jews has been devastating.
“If we can’t condemn acts of terrorism then what are we doing sitting around the table and pretending to sing Kumbaya,” one senior figure, who has been deeply involved in interfaith work, told Plus61J Media.
Muslim New South Wales state legislator Jihad Dib has been a rare exception to the silence from Australian Muslims. He made a statement to his state parliament condemning antisemitic chants at last week’s rally in Sydney.
“Whatever the situation, there is never any justification for the taking of innocent lives…. There are people who cannot sleep tonight for fear. Innocent people in Israel, innocent people in Gaza and their loved ones around the world — every single innocent life matters,” he said.
With reporting by Haaretz.

TITLE: Archaeological, biblical institutions condemn Hamas massacre
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-17T16:15:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/archaeology/2023-10-17/ty-article/archaeological-biblical-institutions-condemn-hamas-massacre/0000018b-3d42-d101-a9ab-bf7e03f60000

Three Western archaeological and biblical study institutions released statements this week condemning Hamas’ massacre of over 1,000 civilians in southern Israel on Saturday October 7.
The American Society for Overseas Research and the U.S.-based Society of Biblical Literature issued statements of support for Israel on Monday, calling the acts of terrorism Hamas perpetrated “evil” and “horrific.” The European Association of Biblical Studies also issued a statement, on Tuesday, calling the scale of Hamas’ attacks on southern Israel “truly shocking.”
However, their statements came after days of protests from Israeli researchers and archaeologists at the failure to officially react to the events of October 7, when Hamas launched an attack on southern Israel at dawn, killing more than 1,300 people.
ASOR is a nonprofit organization founded in 1900 by a collaboration of American universities. Located in Alexandria, Virginia, its purpose is to “initiate, encourage, and support research into, and public understanding of, the history and cultures of the Near East and wider Mediterranean world.” It maintains institutes for research outside the United States, including in Israel.
“ASOR, the American Society for Overseas Research, condemns in the strongest possible terms Hamas’ vicious massacre of more than a thousand innocent non-combatant Israelis on Saturday, October 7, 2023,” the organization stated. “ASOR is an organization that fosters a community of scholars across borders. Our mission is to initiate, encourage, and support research into, and public understanding of, the history and cultures of the Near East and wider Mediterranean world. ASOR is apolitical and has no religious affiliation. ASOR has a large and diverse membership that does not speak with one voice about world politics.
“We believe strongly that recent attacks by Hamas on Israeli civilians are not politics, but evil acts of terrorism. We agree and reaffirm with the president of the United States that Israel has the right and duty to protect its citizens. We also concur with a recent statement by President Biden that ‘the extreme elements of Hamas don’t represent all the Palestinian people,’” ASOR stated.
“We grieve deeply with our Israeli colleagues. We also recognize that there is great suffering in Gaza and among the Palestinian people. We are deeply concerned for the well-being of civilians on all sides of the crisis. It is our hope that all of us will recognize and respect our common humanity,” ASOR concluded its statement.
The society also said that due to developments, it is changing the format of its annual meeting scheduled for November 15-18, at the Hilton Chicago hotel. Presentations at the conference may be attended in person or by Zoom instead of the initial plan to hold a separate virtual component at a different time, ASOR said.
“Israeli archaeologists are among the most significant components of ASOR,” said Bar-Ilan University’s Prof. Aren Maeir, a leading Israeli archaeologist. “There is always a very large Israeli contingent at ASOR meetings.”
Also Monday, the Atlanta-based Society of Biblical Literature, which is devoted to the critical academic investigation of the Bible, stated: “The Society of Biblical Literature (SBL) vigorously condemns the terrorist attacks in Israel initiated by Hamas on October 7, 2023. The slaughter of innocents, taking of hostages, wanton destruction, and the ongoing atrocities against civilian non-combatants are horrific and opposed to the values we espouse as human beings and as a professional society dedicated to the advancement of scholarship on the Bible.
“We are concerned by the subsequent upsurge in antisemitic violence in the United States and globally, and encourage each one of you, our scholarly community, to stand firm against such actions in your own academic institutions. As a professional organization, we stand in solidarity with the people of Israel and wish to support all impacted by these tragic events, especially our members and their families. SBL resolves to develop appropriate educational media, publications, and conferences challenging the use of biblical and other authoritative texts to justify hatred and intolerance in any form.
“As SBL’s governing board, we pledge our support and send strength to members of our organization in Israel whose family members are missing or held hostage by Hamas in Gaza, and we mourn with our colleagues impacted by these tragic events and all other innocent victims of the conflict,” the society stated.
On Tuesday, the European Association of Biblical Studies joined those condemning the atrocities, it said, stating: “The scale of the terror attacks by Hamas in Israel has been truly shocking. We stand with and offer our support to our members and colleagues in Biblical Studies, Archaeology, and related disciplines in Israel, where many of us have studied, lived or worked. And we hope for the immediate release of all hostages, respect for the lives of innocent civilians, and a swift end to violence.”
The statement was signed by the association’s president, George Brooke.
The statements came over a week after Israeli archaeologists and researchers began to contact ASOR, seeking a reaction, Maeir said. He himself co-signed a letter addressed to all ASOR board members and management, urging they take a side.
“At the end of the letter I wrote that they should know that among Israeli archaeologists, some say that if ASOR doesn’t come out with a clear-cut condemnation, Israeli archaeologists would stop their membership in ASOR, stop going to their conferences, stop collaborating with them and maybe urge the Israel Antiquities Authority to prevent ASOR members from getting licenses in Israel on the grounds that it can’t support Hamas supporters.”
Other archaeologists from Israeli universities also wrote in. In parallel, the Society of Biblical Literature was petitioned to react.
“A lot of Israeli archaeologists go to SBL conferences as well, presenting their work on biblical archaeology,” Maeir said. “Their statement is to the point. But I acknowledge that ASOR has a problem in that some of its members are from Arab countries." That could explain the delay, he added.
Also, although these organizations are relatively familiar with the region, Maeir said that “we ourselves are only beginning to understand what happened” in communities bordering Gaza. “To some extent they were also reeling,” he added, and also have to find their way through all the disinformation online.

SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-17T21:22:00+03:00

Israel has strongly denied that it was responsible for the explosion at a packed hospital in Gaza City on Tuesday, saying that a failed missile launch by Palestinian Islamic Jihad was responsible for the carnage.
The Hamas-run Health Ministry said that hundreds of people were killed in what it alleged was an Israeli airstrike. Photos from Al-Ahli Hospital showed fire engulfing the hospital halls, shattered glass and body parts scattered across the area. The ministry said at least 500 people had been killed.
Israeli civilian and military leaders were quick to deny responsibility, with videos of an alleged Islamic Jihad missile launch being widely disseminated on social media.
Breaking: IDF Spokesperson From the analysis of the operational systems of the IDF, an enemy rocket barrage was carried out towards Israel, which passed through the vicinity of the hospital when it was hit. According to intelligence information, from several sources we have,

On Wednesday, the Israeli army released aerial photos to prove that there were no signs of Israeli planes striking the hospital.
פגיעת שיגור כושל של ארגון הטרור גא"פ באזור בית החולים אלמעמדאני בעיר עזה מצורף סרטון מתוך מערכות חה״א שמתעד את אזור בית החולים לפני ואחרי השיגור הכושל של ארגון הטרור גא״פ:
According to IDF Spokesperson Daniel Hagari, who briefed the foreign press early Wednesday, the army's assessment is based on "intelligence information from several sources." The statement goes on to say that "from the analysis of the IDF's operational systems, an enemy rocket barrage was launched towards Israel and passed in the vicinity of the hospital when it was hit."
Hagari added that "intelligence from a few sources that we have in our hands indicates that Islamic Jihad is responsible for the failed rocket launch which hit the hospital in Gaza. I repeat, this is the responsibility of Islamic jihad that killed innocents in the hospital in Gaza."
Hagari added that Israel has audio recordings of telephone conversations between Hamas members in which they implicate Islamic Jihad in the explosion.
"Categorically we do not strike any sensitive facilities - definitely not hospitals. Very much aware of the presence of civilians," IDF International Spokesperson Jonathan Conricus told CNN.
The U.S. Department of Defense declined to address the mass casualty event at the Gaza hospital, though Pentagon spokesperson Sabrina Singh charged Hamas with "putting their command and control units inside hospitals."
She added that the U.S. has "no confirmation" on who bears responsibility, shortly before Israel blamed a failed Islamic Jihad launch.
A spokesman for Islamic denied the Israeli allegations.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog harshly criticized media outlets for their coverage of the devastating explosion. "An Islamic Jihad missile has killed many Palestinians at a Gazan hospital - a place where lives should be saved," Herzog wrote on X, the social media platform formerly known as Twitter. Attached is a visual related to the failed rocket launch by the Islamic Jihad that hit the Al Ahli hospital:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, said that “the barbaric terrorists in Gaza are responsible for the attack on the Gaza hospital, not the IDF. The people who brutally murdered our children are murdering their own children too.”
U.S. President Joe Biden, who is on his way Israel for a historic war-time visit, said that he was "outraged and deeply saddened" by the explosion.
Biden said that he has spoken with King Abdullah II of Jordan and Prime Minister Netanyahu of Israel, adding that he has "directed national security team to continue gathering information about what exactly happened. The United States stands unequivocally for the protection of civilian life during conflict and we mourn the patients, medical staff and other innocents killed or wounded in this tragedy."
Palestinian security forces fired tear gas and stun grenades to disperse protesters in the West Bank city of Ramallah who were throwing rocks and chanting against Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas as popular anger boiled.
The explosion drew condemnation across the Arab world, and protests were staged at Israel's embassies in Turkey and Jordan and near the U.S. embassy in Lebanon, where security forces fired tear gas toward demonstrators.
Television footage showed protests in Yemen's southwestern city of Taz, as well as in the Moroccan and Iraqi capitals.
Lebanon's Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group denounced what it said was Israel's deadly attack on the Al-Ahli al-Arabi hospital in Gaza, run by the Anglican church, and called for "a day of unprecedented anger" against Israel and Biden's visit.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was horrified by the deaths of hundreds of people in a strike on a hospital in Gaza, as Israel and Palestinians traded blame over who was responsible.
"Hospitals and medical personnel are protected under international humanitarian law," Guterres wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter.
UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said she was "horrified" by the Gaza hospital attack without ascribing blame to either party.
"While details are still emerging and bodies are still being counted, the scenes on the ground are devastating," she said, adding "attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, such as hospitals, are unacceptable and must cease now."
Several hospitals in Gaza City have become refuges for hundreds of people, hoping they would be spared bombardment after Israel ordered all residents of the city and surrounding areas to evacuate to the southern Gaza Strip.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas said early on Wednesday that targeting Al-Ahli hospital is a "hideous war massacre" that cannot be tolerated, adding that any talks about anything else rather than stopping the war is unacceptable.
"Israel has crossed all red lines. ... We will not leave nor allow anyone to expel us from there", he added.
The Episcopal Diocese of Jerusalem, which owned and operated the Al-Ahli Hospital where hundreds were killed in a mass casualty event, condemned the "atrocious attack ... in the strongest terms."
"Initial reports suggest the loss of countless lives, a manifestation of what can only be described as a crime against humanity. Hospitals, by the tenets of international humanitarian law, are sanctuaries, yet this assault has transgressed those sacred boundaries," said the diocese about Gaza's only independent, Christian-led medical facility.
"Regrettably, Gaza remains bereft of safe havens. We assert unequivocally that this is deserving international condemnation and retribution. An urgent appeal resonates for the international community to fulfill its duty in protecting civilians and ensuring that such inhumane horrific acts are not replicated," the diocese added.

TITLE: Gaza rockets resume after Biden visit, Netanyahu vows to 'change the equation' in Hamas war
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-18T07:12:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-18/ty-article-live/israeli-army-blames-islamic-jihad-for-hitting-gaza-hospital-in-deadly-strike/0000018b-40a6-d881-abab-edae5c5d0000

Updates
Member of Hamas' political bureau reportedly killed in Israeli strike
A senior member of Hamas' political bureau, Jamila al-Shanti, was killed in an Israeli attack in Gaza, according to reports from the Strip.
It is not clear whether the killing was a deliberate assassination, according to the report. Al-Shanti is the first woman to hold the position, and is considered a senior member of Hamas.
Palestinian killed by Israeli army fire in West Bank, Palestinian Red Crescent says
The Red Crescent reported this morning that a Palestinian was killed by live fire from Israeli security forces in the West Bank town of Ni'lin.
According to the report, 15 more Palestinians were wounded overnight during clashes with the Israeli army.
Senior Hamas official arrested in West Bank, Palestinians say
A wave of arrests across the West Bank led to clashes with dozens of young people overnight, with a senior Hamas official in the West Bank among those arrested, according to Palestinian reports.
Hamas leader Sheikh Hassan Yousef was arrested by Israeli forces at his home in Beitunia.
Palestinians: Two killed in clashes in West Bank refugee camps
Palestinian sources say that two people were killed overnight in clashes in refugee camps close to the West Bank towns of Tul Karm and Dahayshah. According to the reports, there were a number of injuries in both locations.
24-year-old Palestinian killed by Israeli forces in West Bank
A 24-year-old Palestinian man who was shot on Wednesday by Israeli troops in the West Bank has died of his wounds, according to the Palestinian Health Minister. Ibrahim al-Hajj Ali was shot in the stomach during clashes with soldiers near Nablus.
Top State Dept. official resigns in protest at U.S. policy on Israel-Gaza
A top, long-time U.S. State Department official resigned this week in protest of the Biden administration's policy on the Israel-Gaza war and its "impulsive reaction built on confirmation bias, political convenience, intellectual bankruptcy and bureaucratic inertia."
Josh Paul, who worked for the State Department office that approves arms transfers, posted a resignation letter on LinkedIn decrying both the Hamas attack as well as potential escalation by Hezbollah or Iran.
"But I believe to the core of my soul that the response Israel is taking, and with it the American support both for that response, and for the status quo of the occupation, will only lead to more and deeper suffering for both the Israeli and the Palestinian people — and is not in the long-term American interest," he wrote.
"Blind support for one side is destructive in the long term to the interests of the people on both sides," he continued, adding "I fear we are repeating the same mistakes we have made these past decades and I decline to be a part of it for longer."
IDF hits Hezbollah targets in southern Lebanon
The IDF said that it has been attacking Hezbollah targets in southern Lebanon for the past several hours, in response to anti-tank fire into Israeli territory. Among the positions targeted, according to the statement, was an observation point in southwestern Lebanon, from which anti-tank fire was directed at the Israeli border town of Rosh Hanikra on Wednesday.
Germany military plane carrying 19 Israelis lands in Berlin
A German military transport plane carrying 19 Israeli nationals has landed in Berlin, according to the DPA news agency. The Germany military confirmed that an Airbus 350 landed at 11 P.M. local time. Thus far, Germany has transported more than 300 people out of Israel because of the fighting.
Sanders blocks Republican attempt to delay U.S. aid to Gaza
Sen. Bernie Sanders blocked Republican efforts to fast-track legislation preventing the Biden administration from spending its newly announced $100 million in humanitarian aid for the Palestinians.
Republican Sen. Rick Scott attempted to pass via unanimous consent his "Stop Taxpayer Funding of Hamas Act," which would have prevented the money from being spent until Biden would clear a series of restrictions, including certifying with congressional committees that the money wouldn't be spent in a way that would benefit Hamas.
The White House noted in its original statement that the aid would be provided through "trusted partners including UN agencies and international NGOs" — undoubtedly attempting to preempt any accusations that the aid violates the Taylor Force Act, which prohibits U.S. funding to the Palestinian Authority over its payments to convicted terrorists and their families.
"Half of the people in Gaza are children," Sanders said, blocking Scott's maneuver. "I implore you: Do not take Hamas' inhumanity, brutality and terrorism against children."

TITLE: Israeli army presents video, audio to show Islamic Jihad responsible for Gaza hospital blast
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-18T12:55:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-18/ty-article/israeli-army-presents-video-audio-to-show-islamic-jihad-behind-gaza-hospital-blast/0000018b-41f1-d242-abef-53f7d6570000

At a news conference on Wednesday, Israel Defense Forces Spokesman Daniel Hagari categorically denied allegations by Hamas that Tuesday’s explosion at the Al-Ahli Hospital in Gaza City, which reportedly killed hundreds, was the result of an Israeli airstrike.
Late Tuesday, the IDF announced that it had reviewed available data and concluded that it was the result of an Islamic Jihad rocket aimed at Israel that misfired and fell to the ground in Gaza City.
There was no evidence of a direct hit on the hospital building itself, no structural damage to nearby buildings and no bomb crater, which would have been consistent with damage from Israel Air Force aerial bombing, Hagari said on Wednesday.
פגיעת שיגור כושל של ארגון הטרור גא"פ באזור בית החולים אלמעמדאני בעיר עזה מצורף סרטון מתוך מערכות חה״א שמתעד את אזור בית החולים לפני ואחרי השיגור הכושל של ארגון הטרור גא״פ:
"According to our intelligence, Hamas checked reports and understood it was a Palestinian Islamic Jihad misfire, then launched a global media campaign with inflated numbers of casualties," the IDF spokesman said. "They understood with absolute certainty that it was a rocket launched by Palestinian Islamic Jihad."
The Hamas-run Health Ministry in Gaza said that hundreds of people were killed in what it alleged was an Israeli airstrike. Photos from Al-Ahli Hospital showed fire engulfing the hospital halls, shattered glass and body parts scattered across the area. The ministry said at least 500 people had been killed.
Attached is a recording of a conversation between Hamas operatives regarding the Islamic Jihad failed rocket launch on the hospital on October 17, 2023:
"It is impossible to know what happened as quickly as Hamas claimed they knew," Hagari said. "That should have been an initial warning sign." Israel also has audio recordings of telephone conversations between Hamas members in which they implicate Islamic Jihad in the explosion, Hagari added.
Amid the thousands of rockets that have been fired at Israeli population centers since the war between Israel and Hamas and its allies in Gaza began a week and a half ago, 450 rockets fired from Gaza have fallen short, landing inside the Strip, Hagari noted.
"Categorically we do not strike any sensitive facilities, definitely not hospitals. Very much aware of the presence of civilians," IDF international spokesperson Jonathan Conricus told CNN.
The deaths on Tuesday at the Al-Ahli Hospital have provoked rage in the Arab world, where the allegations against Israel have been widely accepted, and expressions of deep concern among Western leaders.
U.S. President Joe Biden, who landed in Israel on Wednesday for a lightning wartime visit, said that he was "outraged and deeply saddened" by the explosion. The president said he has "directed the national security team to continue gathering information about what exactly happened. The United States stands unequivocally for the protection of civilian life during conflict and we mourn the patients, medical staff and other innocents killed or wounded in this tragedy."
“Based on what I’ve seen, it appears as though it was done by the other team, not you,” Biden told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a meeting in Israel Wednesday. But Biden said there were “a lot of people out there” who weren’t sure what caused the blast.
Palestinian Islamic Jihad rejected the Israeli military spokesman's statement that a failed rocket launch was the source of the explosion and claimed that "the angle of the impact and the intensity of the fire proves that it was an attack from the air."
Islamic Jihad said that "the hospitals in the Gaza Strip received evacuation notices before they were hit by the bombings, but no one in the international community intervened," adding that "Israel is spreading [contradictory] versions [of events], saying Israeli Foreign Ministry spokesman Lior Ben-Dor said that the hospital housed weapons but the Israeli army attributed it to a failed rocket launch.
Islamic Jihad also stated that "just as Israel has previously abdicated responsibility for the crimes it committed, including the injury to journalist Shireen Abu-Akleh, this is repeating itself now as well."
The reference is to the Al Jazeera reporter who was killed while covering an Israeli military raid in Jenin on May 11, 2022. Although the IDF initially denied any involvement in the killing, it later conceded that Abu Akleh was most likely killed by Israeli fire.

TITLE: Russian state media calls Israeli retaliation in Gaza 'fascism', demands sanctions over evacuation order
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-18T14:16:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-18/ty-article/russian-media-calls-israeli-retaliation-in-gaza-fascism-demands-sanctions/0000018b-423e-d242-abef-523e7d060000

Margarita Simonyan, the editor-in-chief of the Russian network RT and one of the Kremlin’s top propagandists, accused Israel of “fascism” over its military operation in Gaza this week, during a television appearance in which she railed at Jewish expatriates in Israel for their alleged disloyalty.
“How can the leaders of the Jewish nation, Israel, say that everyone in Palestine is responsible and call all of them animals that resemble humans,” she asked, according to a translation of her remarks during an appearance on popular presenter Vladimir Solovyov’s state television program published by Russian Media Monitor.
“This is fascism,” Simonyan asserted, accusing Israel and the Palestinians of “horrifying cruelty” and claiming that, unlike Israel, in Russia “there is no hatred and no rejection of a nation.”
Russian officials and state media figures have repeatedly called for the dissolution of Ukraine as a sovereign state—while Russian troops have been implicated in numerous war crimes against Ukrainian civilians.
Simonyan also railed against Russian expatriates critical of Russia’s war such as musician Andrey Makarevich, arguing that those who expressed support for Israel while opposing the invasion of Ukraine were hypocrites whose principles were selectively applied.
Makarevich, a Russian Jew and founder of the Russian rock band Mashina Vremeni, moved to Israel in 2022 in the wake of Russia’s invasion, telling Radio Free Europe that supporters of the war can “fuck off.”
Such people have “been trying to convince us that their main issue with Russia is Putin…because we contradict their principles…they are for peace,” Simonyan said. But “as soon as things flared up in Israel, all of it suddenly vanished…the pacifism suddenly disappeared.”
For his part, Solovyov—who has long used his Jewish identity to give weight to Russian President Vladimir Putin's talking points—demanded that Israel be sanctioned for calling for Palestinians in Gaza to evacuate their homes and for maintaining a nuclear arsenal.
Writing for the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), Russian Media Monitor’s Julia Davis noted that while Solovyov has previously criticized Hamas for its murder of over 1,400 Israelis, many other “Kremlin-endorsed propagandists celebrated the fighting as a distraction to tear the West’s eyes from Ukraine.”
Military correspondent Dmitry Steshin, she noted, “posted on his Telegram channel Russky Tarantas that there should be ‘not a drop of pity or sympathy” for Israelis’ including former Russian citizens” derisively describing Russian-Israelis as “relocants.”
Putin has long used allegations of Nazism and antisemitism to legitimize his actions against Ukraine. Following his invasion of Crimea in 2014, the Russian president cited an alleged “rampage” of reactionary, nationalistic and antisemitic forces across the country — and over the next several years, Russian state media featured a steady stream of false reports about Ukrainian attacks on local Jews.
Since last year’s invasion, however, this rhetoric has shifted, with the Kremlin attempting to position the Russian people as the new Jews under attack, with Simonyan declaring that “the Russian is your new kike. You want to burn us all in an oven.”
Европеец, ты как есть скажи, Не молчи: Русский для вас - это новый жид. Сжечь бы нас всех в печи. Новая песня Шнура. Все так и есть, конечно.
Both Russia and Ukraine have blamed each other, without providing any evidence, for arming Hamas.
In a recent post on X (formerly Twitter), Dmitry Medvedev, a former Russian President now serving as Deputy Chairman of the country’s Security Council, claimed that “the weapons handed to the nazi regime in Ukraine are now being actively used against Israel.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has repeatedly called for international support for Israel’s war against Hamas, in turn asserted that "Russia is interested in triggering a war in the Middle East, so that a new source of pain and suffering could undermine world unity, increase discord and contradictions, and thus help Russia destroy freedom in Europe."

TITLE: "We have become a connection point for millions of artists from around the world"
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-18T14:59:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/haaretz-labels/music-technology/2023-10-18/ty-article-labels/.premium/we-have-become-a-connection-point-for-millions-of-artists-from-around-the-world/0000018b-42a2-df22-a5eb-4bfb60c00000

Ori Winokur, head of the music and sound department at Artlist, does not see artificial intelligence as a threat to video and music creators, but a tool that will help them create more effectively. And that is actually also the story of Artlist itself, a creative and technology company that started as a place where every video editor can enjoy licensed music, and has since become a creative tool through catalogs of sound, video, images and original music. "Our system also knows how to recommend an optimal connection between the catalogs. We are constantly developing and evolving so that every user has quality content," says Winokur.
Artlist began from a personal need of Ira Belsky, one of the founders and currently co-CEO of the company: "It was a big challenge to find quality music, at an affordable price, that video editors could use in their videos. The licenses were complicated, and I sensed that there was a demand here that was not being met."
The difficulty Belsky encountered coincided with a policy change elsewhere – YouTube, which in 2013 was transformed from a place of collaboration and free use to a content identification platform with enormous advertising potential. YouTube's ability to identify content and users and target them, both in terms of music and advertising, led major music labels to demand their share as copyright holders. As a result, millions of pieces of music were blocked, and those affected, among others, were independent video editors who could no longer use the music freely. "Together with two talented musician friends, Assi Ayalon and Eyal Raz, and a friend from the technological side who today serves as co-CEO with me, Itzik Elbaz, we decided to start a website with a catalog of quality pieces of music at an affordable price," he says.
In 2016 Belsky and the musician Assi Ayalon transformed this clear need that arose from the field and created Artlist, which offered a licensed music catalog under an innovative subscription model, essentially eliminating the need for the independent video editor to deal legally with the various creators, managers and labels. "The four friends built a website with a catalog of music, and the need for it was so strong that within two weeks the company was already profitable, and from there it just kept growing at a very fast pace until it became the successful global company it is today," says Winokur.
The AI that helped the creative
What started with the connection between sound and video has developed over the years and has become more essential in a reality where each of us is actually a video editor who can shoot with a smartphone. Artlist offers all types of music at fair prices, and has created another tool where the user can find everything they need in one place.
Artlist reports more than 20 million registered subscribers, including major companies as well as private content creators, who can access everything it offers without limitation: catalogs of music, sound effects, images– visualization, video clips for editors to incorporate in editing, templates as a basis for video editing – which even Justin Timberlake used for his album cover – as well as software and editing tools.
The company, which continues to grow at an accelerated rate, even acquired in 2020 the American company MotionArray, which is a marketplace for video creators, and includes templates, presets, plugins, video transitions, design graphics and graphic animations ready for video editing software. A year later, Artlist also acquired the British software company FXhome, thereby positioning itself alongside companies such as Adobe Global that provide a comprehensive solution that includes editing tools and digital media.
By managing a number of large and leading products, Artlist has become a major player in the field of content creation, with more than 400 employees in Israel and around the world working in creative, technology, content, data, research and development, music, video, marketing and more. The company says that today its customers include influencers and global brands, such as Coca-Cola, Nike, Google, IKEA, Netflix and more.
"For years we've been using AI support to locate and connect content," says Winokur. "We're working on AI features where a creator will write what he's working on and receive suggestions for music, sound effects, images and video. Already today we have a semantic search on the entire catalog, so the system understands what the search request is even if the term is written in a way that does not match how we defined it. Our emphasis is on our artists, on quality content and on a high-level supply so that we will provide a comprehensive solution for anyone who wants to create content."
He adds that artificial intelligence serves creative people who will turn it into a work tool: "Artlist uses AI technology for the benefit of search and further developments. It may change the definitions of editing or the creative process as we know it, but it will also make it possible to stretch boundaries and achieve a different creative level. Also, in using artificial intelligence we will need people to build the basis of the story, and we see it as a useful tool and not one that will damage us."
Paving a way for artists
The way Artlist operates accurately reflects the connection between its founders: Ira Belsky, who was an independent video creator, Itzik Elbaz, who came from the world of technology, Eyal Raz and Assi Ayalon, who were music producers.
A few years ago, the company added another layer to its services to expand the variety of quality content for users, adding original video and music productions under Artlist Original – Artlist's original music production label, which produces more than 2,000 songs a year, and includes independent artists from around the world. The company provides direct support throughout the content production and distribution process. "We have become a connection point for hundreds of independent and active artists from all over the world, and we act as their label, produce the music and manage their rights," says Winokur.
And what does the future hold? Belski shares: "The developments we are planning in the near future – will continue. We want to give creators everything they need to create the best video content, and be a platform for artists to distribute their works and receive adequate remuneration, which allows them to do what they love."

TITLE: Watch: The videos behind Gaza hospital rocket blast – and what they show
SOURCE: haaretz

TITLE: ‘If she’s in the hands of Hamas, we don’t know how she’ll survive with Crohn’s’
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-18T18:55:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-18/ty-article-magazine/if-shes-in-the-hands-of-hamas-we-dont-know-how-shell-survive-with-crohns/0000018b-4328-de3d-a58f-cb693a160000

Tamar Gutman didn’t leave the house much in recent years. The 27-year-old Israeli suffered from repeated attacks of Crohn’s disease, a debilitating inflammatory bowel illness that required multiple hospitalizations and constant medication. On Friday October 6, though, she realized a small dream: Together with four close friends, she planned to attend the Supernova music festival near Kibbutz Re’im.
"She went with Ben, Dor, Yiftah and Eden. They're a group, they're together all the time," says her older sister, Dr. Adva Gutman-Tirosh. “They live in the same community, hang out in each other’s homes – most of the time in Tamar’s house. They cook and eat together. She would send them shopping, they cleaned the house for her. This was a big celebration and she decided that this time she was going.”
Yaira Gutman, Tamar’s mother, adds: “Until now she was too weak and couldn’t drink alcohol [to attend]. But she really wanted to go to this festival. With our black humor these days, we talked about the fact that when the shooting began Adva wrote and told her to flee – but even when she’s walking she cries every 100 meters that she’s too tired, so where exactly could she run to?”
Tamar, who was studying law at Ono Academic College, was born in Kfar Bin Nun, a moshav in central Israel. Her parents – David, an engineer, and Yaira, formerly an operating room nurse – and her three sisters still live there. She recently moved to the nearby moshav of Beit Hashmonai, but her mother and sisters Neta and Adva say she was still at her parents’ house most of the time.
She had trouble holding down a regular job or going to college because of her Crohn’s disease, but in the past year the disease regressed somewhat, and she was able to study and complete her first year of law school, scoring good grades.
27-year-old Tamar Gutman from Kfar Bin Nun was abducted by Hamas terrorists from the Supernova party near Re'im, in southern Israel, on October 7. She is a law student, and suffers from debilitating Crohn's disease attacks.
“She was on a high,” says younger sister Neta, 24. “Things went well for her in the past year, and she flourished and was about to begin her second year of studies. She also received money from the National Insurance Institute, which gave her some breathing space because she barely worked. She didn’t like asking our parents for money but felt she was returning to life, excited by the happiness of the past year.”
Tattooed on Tamar’s belly is a pretty drawing of an orchid and a quote in English that sums her up: “Die with memories, not dreams.”
The eve of the music festival was also the eve of the Simchat Torah Jewish holiday. Tamar contacted her mother, who was in Cyprus, and reminded her that there was no food for her father, who remained at home in Kfar Bin Nun, nor for 38-year-old Adva (who’s studying for the final exam in her medical specialty, orthopedics, and is also the mother of two young children). Younger sister Neta had left two days earlier for a year’s work with a family in Boston, but was only in America for three days before rushing back to Israel. Her other sister, Ella, 35, was in Sinai with her children.
“We were guilty of leaving father without food because we were busy with Neta’s trip. Tamar found out – which is classic Tamar. In other words, we can starve him and starve Adva who’s studying, but Tamar is different,” says her mother. “I received a phone call in Cyprus: ‘Do you remember that it’s the eve of a holiday, and Dad and Adva are alone without food?’
“I told her, ‘You have a credit card, take care of it.’ So she bought food and brought it to her father and sat with him for a holiday meal, and then she went to Adva to bring them food and to say hi.”
When Tamar arrived, Adva couldn’t help but notice her younger sister’s shiny new nail polish. “We talked about the festival, about what she would wear – jeans and a black crop top. I laughed a little at the nail polish she’d had done especially for it: metallic silver that you couldn’t possibly miss. Usually we don’t agree on matters of taste, Tamar and I; we’re very different in appearance. But that nail polish was actually good, came out really nicely. And in hindsight, that nail polish helped me realize that she wasn’t lying wounded in a hospital.”
‘She didn’t sound scared enough’
At 6:30 A.M. on Saturday October 7, the sirens began wailing in Kfar Bin Nun. “My children were with my husband Gideon’s parents in Ramat Gan,” Adva recounts. “My husband and I ran to the safe room and then I sent a message to Tamar: ‘How are you doing? Leave the festival and drive straight to Dad’s’ – because my father has a safe room and she doesn’t. Because I thought that if we had sirens, then certainly there were sirens in the Gaza border communities, and I knew that the festival was in that area. She responded at 7:06, spending a couple of minutes saying that there were people there who were shooting and they were told not to travel on the highway.
“I wrote her: ‘In both directions? Drive wherever they let you drive. Don’t stay where you are.’ And she replied, ‘Yes, a security guard was shot.’
“She still hadn’t seen terrorists at this point. I wrote: ‘Tell me where you’re going, I’ll find a place for you to be.’ And then: ‘Is there someone armed with you? Is there a security force? Look carefully where you’re sitting and where you can hide, and answer me so I won’t worry.’
“She was worried about us and asked whether we heard sirens too. I wrote: ‘Constantly.’ And then she replied in a recorded message. I’ll play it for you.”
Adva plays the recording by Tamar, who doesn’t sound anxious or nervous. Her complacency concerned Adva, though.
“She didn’t sound scared enough to me and I wanted her to be more worried,” she says. “She wrote that there was shooting from the road. I wrote to her that on the news they said there were many terrorists in the area. I wanted her to be ready and I repeatedly wrote, ‘Look very carefully where you flee to.’
 
“She replied that they weren’t leaving. I wrote: ‘If you can, sit next to someone with whom you can hide, preferably someone with a gun and preferably not in a group of people’ – because I thought that if there was shooting, the first shots would be into a concentration of people. I already understood that the incident wasn’t under control. Then I sent another message that she didn’t see. 
“Later, when we received her phone, I saw that she had written she was on her way home and that they were shooting at the car. That was the point at which the terrorists were coming from all directions.”
Tamar’s phone was located on the exit route from the festival. The police returned it to the family.
At this point on the Saturday, Adva began to receive messages from her fellow medical students.
“One of my girlfriends is an army doctor and she said she was going to the area. I asked her to look for Tamar and let me know what was happening. And she said: ‘You don’t understand how much chaos there is here.’
“I started sending messages to all my friends at Soroka and Barzilai [medical centers in Be’er Sheva and Ashkelon, respectively]. I sent pictures. And when I saw that it wasn’t contained and Tamar didn’t reply, I decided to go myself to Soroka to look for her, because I understood that most of the wounded were arriving there.”
When Adva arrived, she says she donned her doctor’s uniform so she could enter the emergency room. “Everyone there knows me; I worked and studied there. I started to look for her. I circulated among the doctors and later among all the wounded with pictures of her and tried to ask if they had seen her. There was terrible chaos there and there were many orthopedic patients who were lying and waiting to be treated, because they were slightly or moderately wounded.
“So I also tended to anyone I could for a while. One of the doctors to whom I showed Tamar’s picture told me: ‘I think I saw her in neurosurgery.’ And my heart sank because neurosurgery means head injuries. I hoped he was mistaken. I went up there and he showed me the wounded woman whom he thought resembled Tamar. From a distance I saw her nail polish and told him: ‘It’s not her.’ I was so happy at that moment that she had come a day earlier to show me her nail polish.”
Adva couldn’t find Tamar in any hospital, nor did she find anyone who had seen her. Her four friends – Ben, Dor, Yiftah and Eden – had also disappeared.
At the same time, her mother was trying to get a plane ticket in order to return to Israel.
‘It’s all connections’
“I was at a competition in Cyprus,” says Yaira. “I’m a dragon boat paddler. It’s a rowboat with two rows of paddlers on each side – a good health activity for women recovering from breast cancer. That same morning someone said: ‘There’s chaos in Israel.’ My second-eldest daughter, Ella, was in Sinai, and I was worried about that, so I spent all morning trying to get her out of Sinai. And only after I succeeded did I wonder what was happening with the other girls and why they hadn’t sent me a flower icon – because we have a family tradition that when there’s a siren, we send an emoji in the family group so we’ll all know everything’s okay. And then Adva called and said, ‘Mom, I didn’t want to tell you but Tamar has been missing since 8 A.M.’”
Yaira started searching from afar and also started asking for help from contacts in order to try to find Tamar.
“Adva managed everything in Israel and I tried on the level of friends searching for her in hiding places. We didn’t understand the dimensions of the attack and were convinced she had fled like everyone else, and at most had been injured. And when I arrived in Israel and understood what Adva was doing, I said: ‘You’re giving everyone tasks, but I’m going down there to try to locate her phone’ – because we thought the fighting was over already. When we arrived, we discovered that the fighting wasn’t over.”
In the days following the attack, the Gutmans continued to ask for help from anyone they knew, until they received a clear message that Tamar was now considered a hostage. Friends suggested that they wait patiently, but they opted to launch a media campaign, including interviews with the international press, in order to make sure her name wouldn’t disappear from the news.
A few days ago, they received a phone call from the police unit in charge of collecting information about missing persons (Lahav 433), and an officer said he was now the address for all their questions. Other than him, though, nobody official contacted them, they say.
“Because it’s Israel and we have lots of friends, we reached people in positions of power,” says Adva. “We have connections in the Home Front Command in the national rescue unit, and I also know everyone because I flew to Nepal on a rescue delegation after the earthquake there [in 2015]. I made contact with every possible doctor. It’s all connections.
“But no political figure has contacted us. I met with the Red Cross. They’re supposed to enforce the Geneva Convention, which is why they take care of hostages. But they’re not a political organization and they don’t give us any information. They aren’t intermediaries, and therefore we have no definite information about Tamar.”
The family is particularly concerned because of her medical condition. “She received biological treatment for Crohn’s, and stressful situations are also very bad for her – they cause attacks. And these are serious attacks of intestinal blockage and constant vomiting. If she’s in the hands of Hamas, in terms of her health we don’t know how she’ll survive there,” says Adva.
Of the four friends who were with her at the party, the bodies of two – Yiftah and Eden – have been found. Ben and Dor are still missing, along with Tamar. “They haven’t finished identifying the people who were murdered at the festival yet, they’re far from finishing. The pace of work there is unreasonable,” Adva sighs.
While waiting for some information from the authorities, they decided on a division of labor within the family: Adva manages everything and everyone; the parents and other sisters do whatever they can. Among other things, they have to deal with lots of rumors and fake information from all kinds of places, says Yaira.
“At first they told us her name is on all kinds of lists of survivors hiding in kibbutzim, but it wasn’t. Then they said she’s on the list of hostages, but it turned out there’s no such list. Two days ago, a friend of Tamar’s from the Home Front Command called and said they had finished identifying all the bodies, and messages were being sent to the families.
“We lit all the lights in the house and the street lamps outside and waited, crushed. And only Adva said: ‘I don’t think so, it’s not logical.’ She and Gideon asked for help from everyone possible and reached the commander of the corps, who said: ‘What are you talking about? They haven’t finished even a third.’ So we made a family decision that we won’t get emotional about any message until Adva and Gideon check it out. Because they can check. I can also appeal to my connections, but I want to remain a mother and not to deal with that. We’re crushed to an indescribable degree.”
The Gutman family is strong, supportive and well connected, but they’re not made of steel either. The impossible situation is leaving its mark, admits Yaira, and the lack of attention from the authorities supposedly handling the matter makes everything that much harder. “The burden on Adva is tremendous. She fell apart this morning,” her mother reports.
“It would help if someone official were to contact us and at least say that they don’t know anything – instead of our constantly trying to request help from the whole world in order to receive the same answer,” says Yaira. “If only someone would check that we’re alive. If someone would call and say ‘We see you.’ They didn’t even send us a social worker. We’re all on edge and nobody thinks about that because, after all, they won’t get our children out of Hamas’ clutches in two days. It will take months if not years.
“And we have to make sure that when they get out, there will be someone to receive them. That the families won’t be totally destroyed in the meantime. We have connections and abilities – I don’t know what those who don’t are doing. And we’re also breaking. This morning, after Adva collapsed, my husband pleaded to stop the searches. He said: ‘I can’t lose another child.’”

TITLE: New discovery changes story of King Hazael’s attack on biblical Gath
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-18T20:35:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/archaeology/2023-10-18/ty-article-magazine/new-discovery-changes-story-of-king-hazaels-attack-on-biblical-gath/0000018b-43ab-de3d-a58f-cbeb50e70000

“‘Thou shalt be for fuel to the fire ... thou shalt be no more remembered; for I the Lord have spoken it’” Ezekiel 21:37
Tales of divine wrath expressed in fire, or kings burning cities down, are not rare in the Bible. Indeed, evidence suggesting conflagration has been found at several sites, including in ancient Jerusalem, Gezer – and the Philistine city of Gath (aka Tell es-Safi).
However, techniques commonly used in archaeology are limited in their ability to distinguish mud bricks fired in kilns as opposed to mud bricks baked by enemies burning the city down, let alone fired bricks that subsequently experienced secondary heating by arson. Nor are the usual techniques helpful in studying mud bricks heated to low temperatures less than about 500 degrees Celsius (932 degrees Fahrenheit), or in identifying the temperature they experienced.
Now a collaboration of Israeli archaeologists presents archaeomagnetism as a method not only to date ancient ruins but as a way to distinguish mud bricks fired in kilns as opposed to ones burned by mishap or in war.
The archaeologists Yoav Vaknin, Oded Lipschits and Erez Ben-Yosef of Tel Aviv University with geophysicist Ron Shaar of the Hebrew University, Adi Eliyahu Behar of Ariel University and Aren Maeir of Bar-Ilan University demonstrate the method works in an article in PLOS One. And when the technique was applied to a specific building in the Philistine city of Gath (located halfway between Jerusalem and Ashkelon), it changed the narrative of the city’s fate at the hands of Hazael, king of Aram Damascus (II Kings 12:18).
O give me a home
In the beginning, as we abandoned the cave for the external dwelling, there were huts built from reeds, branches, bones – even mammoth tusks. Construction with mud bricks may have only emerged in the Late Neolithic.
Mud bricks were (and still are) made by kneading straw or grasses into mud. Pine needles will do. The thoroughly massaged mélange is put into molds to set. Once set, the raw brick is unmolded and left to dry for days or even weeks, ideally in the shade rather than in direct sunlight because drying too fast causes them to crack.
The snag is that unfired mud bricks are vulnerable to the elements, such as rain. Which explains the latter-day mania for painting the house every Passover, Prof. Maeir jokes – the only way to keep a mud-brick edifice standing for any time is to plaster the walls and if you don’t do that regularly, the bricks revert into a mud bath. Sun-dried brick structures from antiquity have only survived under extraordinary conditions: archaeologists have found a mud -brick village in Israel’s Jordan Valley from 7,200 years ago.
More robust kiln-fired bricks seem to have emerged perhaps around 7,000 years ago, in Mesopotamia and the Far East (later than the advent of kiln-fired pottery). The biblical story about the Tower of Babel even specifically mentions the technique: “And the whole earth was of one language and of one speech. And it came to pass, as they journeyed east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there. And they said one to another: ‘Come, let us make brick, and burn them thoroughly.’ And they had brick for stone” – Genesis, 11:1-3.
The 11th-century sage Rashi interpreted that to mean that the bricks for the Tower of Babel had been fired in kilns.
“Some claim that mud bricks were being fired in the Levant too, including here, as early as the Iron Age or earlier,” Vaknin says. “But most people think brick firing here only began in the Roman period.”
Why might the Mesopotamians have been firing bricks but not we so near by? Because they lived on a low-lying plain watered by the Euphrates and Tigris and had plenty of water and mud, less stone. So they had to fire their bricks to be like stone.
In the rocky Levant, on the other hand, people built using mud brick for ordinary construction and if a harder material was required – for instance, for foundations – they used stone. In most parts of the country, mud brick was the main building material until the Roman period.
In 2011, the claim was made in the Journal of Archaeological Science that a specific wall in Gath, predating the Roman period by centuries, was apparently constructed using fired bricks: “a most unusual occurrence for this time period in the Levant,” the authors (including Maeir) observed. It was part of a structure that collapsed over years following King Hazael’s attack in about 811 B.C.E., they surmised.
The new technique indicates that this wall was not made of fired bricks, and the building it was in did not gently crumble over years following that Aramean assault. The wall was made of sun-dried mud bricks and the building it was in burned down in a single spasm of violence.
“Throughout the Bronze and Iron Ages, the main building material in most parts of the Land of Israel was mud bricks,” stated Lipschits. “This cheap and readily available material was used to build walls in most buildings, sometimes on top of stone foundations. That’s why it’s so important to understand the technology used in making these bricks.”
The fire rages
This enlightenment is based on the ability of the archaeomagnetic technique to discern when mud bricks have been exposed to fairly low heat, below the temperature at which bricks are typically fired.
A word on temperatures. The kiddies’ Lag Ba’omer bonfire can reach 900 degrees Celsius, and big ones even more; ceramics are fired at least at 800 degrees Celsius (and usually higher, though beyond 1,200-1,300 degrees, the clay melts into a puddle). Even early Neolithic kilns are believed to have reached temperatures as high as 900 Celsius degrees or beyond. Wouldn’t a city set ablaze reach even higher temperatures?
Not necessarily. “When a city burns down, the temperature depends on a lot of factors, including the burnable elements,” Vaknin explains. Some archaeologists even suspect that biblical adversaries might have brought their own fuel to the foul city they wished to eradicate, he adds.
Maeir points out that British forces in Afghanistan in the 19th century encountered difficulty in punitively burning down the traditional mud-brick architecture, and learned that the best way to destroy a mud-brick village was to throw explosives into each house. “What we learn is that this image we have – that invaders would capture a city and rampage with torches and whole place would burn down – is a misconception,” Maeir says. “You have to make an effort.” Though a burning town could theoretically have had hot spots, he adds – for example, stores of flammables like olive, oil and grains.
Either way, the temperatures that develop in a burning building are not uniform and are not necessarily that high, Vaknin says. “For instance, a roof made of mud plaster can reach 500-600 degrees or more, while the floor can be less than 200,” he says, pointing out that heat rises.
Other techniques to analyze ancient bricks rely on changes in the mineral composition: some disappear, some are destroyed, others change, all of which happens at specific temperatures. The color of the brick changes, but all this only happens above about 500 degrees Celsius. The archaeomagnetism method isn’t based on changes in mineral composition but on changes in magnetization.
Come the collapse
The Earth’s magnetosphere constantly fluctuates in intensity and direction. Mud and clay contain ferromagnetic particles that lie in random directions in mud slurry. The ferromagnetic particles in a sun-dried brick will lie in random directions, their signals canceling each other out, and the brick will have only a weak magnetic signal, if any.
But if the mud is heated, as it cools the iron particles line up like tiny compass needles, all pointing in the direction of the magnetosphere at the moment, and they remain in that orientation forever more.
So if bricks have no magnetic signal to speak of, they were sun-dried. If each brick in an ancient wall has a different magnetic orientation, then evidently they were fired in kilns, each brick fired in whichever orientation vis-à-vis the magnetosphere.
And if the bricks in a wall have the same orientation, they were likely heated together and we may surmise that somebody had an epic accident, or the enemy burned the building down.
Crucially, the new technique enables the archaeologists to detect heating below 500 degrees Celsius, which hadn’t been possible using the spectrometric techniques, Maeir adds.
In Gath, for instance, previous work hadn’t detected fire inside the building to which the wall was associated, but it was there. The lower course of mud bricks was shown to have been heated to less than 400 degrees Celsius and higher bricks (again, heat rises) to 500-600 degrees or so, the archaeologists say.
The new technique was also applied to the rubble by said wall, which had been thought to result from decades of decay following the Aramean conquest. The rubble shared that same magnetic orientation as the bricks in the wall, the team found. And thus they could demonstrate that the collapse happened in one dramatic event.
What about fired bricks in a building that then gets burned by the enemy? Double-firing, as it were – can the technology be helpful there too? “If the fire is hot enough, indeed the original magnetization will be erased and the bricks will gain the orientation of the newest conflagration,” Vaknin explains. That is why reconstruction of temperature is key. If a brick demonstrated to have been fired is then found to have been heated to, say, 400 degrees,which is too low for a kiln – we have separate burning events.
And yes, a brick could have been sun-dried, then placed in a structure that was burned down by an invader, and then that could have happened again.
Anyway, all this depends on knowing the magnetic field. How much does the ambient planetary magnetic field change over time? How often? What resolution can be achieved?
Well, we don’t know any of that exactly; research is ongoing, but for now it can be said that if the magnetic signal is statistically different at two sites, then evidently they were not destroyed in the same military campaign. If they have the same signal, they may have been destroyed in the same military campaign, Vaknin says.
So what have we? A technique that can help not only date ancient sites using the magnetic properties of clay pots and bricks, and that can detect the temperature of the heat they experienced, but which ended up changing the narrative of the ferocity of Hazael’s attack on Gath, based on the story of one house. A house that had been thought not to have burned inside, only on the roof, but it did. That house had been thought to have been, strangely, made of fired bricks, but wasn’t; and it didn't collapse over time but abruptly, in one terrible event that left scars in the collective memory:
“Then Hazael king of Aram went up, and fought against Gath” – 2 Kings 12:18.

TITLE: For Hamas, the Gaza hospital tragedy is a narrative victory
SOURCE: haaretz

Depending on what your social media feed looks like right now, you either believe that Israel deliberately struck a Gazan hospital, killing over 500 innocent people, or you believe that while Islamic Jihad was aiming at Israelis, it misfired a rocket that hit the hospital or its parking lot, and Hamas has cynically exploited the explosion for its own media victory.
Haaretz Today
For Hamas, the Gaza Hospital Tragedy Is a Narrative Victory
The mounting evidence points much more strongly to Israel’s version of how the tragedy at Al Ahli Anglican hospital in Gaza City unfolded, but the damage has been done. In the meantime, Gazans will bury their dead, who've become pawns in an international game of influence

TITLE: Israelis need more than a vague demand to ‘destroy Hamas’
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-18T21:09:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-18/ty-article-opinion/israelis-need-more-than-a-vague-demand-to-destroy-hamas/0000018b-43dc-df22-a5eb-4bfdecc10000

On August 14, 1941, during one of the darkest periods of World War II, President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Prime Minister Winston Churchill published the Atlantic Charter. While the swastika flag was flying over the Eiffel Tower and the Acropolis; while Londoners were living in fear of Luftwaffe bombers; and while Nazi tanks were storming toward Moscow, Roosevelt and Churchill looked to the future, and in the Atlantic Charter mapped how they envisioned the world looking after the defeat of Nazism.
The Charter declared that the victorious Allies would not use their triumph to expand their territories, would recognize nations’ rights to self-determination and democratic rule, and would redraw national borders only with the agreement of the local populations. The Charter called for increased global cooperation to improve the lives of all human beings, and to enable all people to live in freedom from fear, violence, and poverty.
The Charter’s ideals were never fully implemented, but they constituted the foundation for a new and better global order, and they explained to millions of Allied soldiers and civilians what they were fighting for and why they were risking their lives. The Atlantic Charter helped to pave the way to the demise of imperialism; the drive toward equality for women, Blacks, Jews, LGBTQ people and other minorities; and also to the establishment of the State of Israel.
In August 1941, Roosevelt and Churchill didn’t just talk vaguely about the need “to destroy Nazism.” Similarly, today, Israelis urgently require something deeper and more constructive than a vague promise "to destroy Hamas." We need an Israeli Charter, to explain how our lives will look after victory is achieved, and the positive goals for which millions of soldiers and civilians are being required to risk and even sacrifice their lives.
Residents of Be’eri and Sderot, of Kfar Azza and Ofakim, need to know that after the victory, the government will unite them and care for their safety, instead of inciting divisions between them – and abandoning all. Non-Jewish citizens of Israel – like the families of Lt. Col. Alim Saad, who fell in battle on the Lebanese front, Abd al-Rahman al-Nasasara, who was murdered by terrorists when he tried to rescue survivors, and Awad Darawshe, who was killed while driving an ambulance – must know that after the victory, they will enjoy full equality. Millions of women who are struggling to hold together families, communities and military positions – like Rachel Edri, who saved her family from the terrorists, Border Police soldier Shifra Buchris, who saved dozens from being massacred, and Lt. Col. Or Ben Yehuda, a battalion commander who has been leading her men and women in battle in recent days – need to know that after the victory, they will not be sent back to the kitchen or enclosed behind screens and veils. LGBTQ soldiers, like Capt. (res.) Sagi Golan, who fell in battle at Be’eri a week before he was due to marry his boyfriend, must know that their relationships will be fully recognized by the state, and that after the victory they will be able to marry officially in the state for which they risk their lives.
Parents need to know that after the victory, schools will teach kids values of peace and love, rather than just war and hate. Journalists, influencers, poets and thinkers need to know that both when the cannons roar and when the cannons fall silent, the muses will never be silenced. Even Palestinians in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, whom Israel requires to show restraint and condemn Hamas, need to know that after Hamas is defeated, a victorious Israel will offer them its hand in peace, and will not exploit that victory to expel them from their lands or trample their rights.
And if this government does dream of exploiting victory to annex territories, forcefully redraw borderlines, expel populations, ignore rights, censor speech, realize messianic fantasies or turn Israel into a theocratic dictatorship – we need to know it now. Don’t tell us that these are divisive issues that should wait until victory is secured; or that there is just no time now to talk about the future. If Roosevelt and Churchill found time in August 1941 to speak about the distant future, our emergency government can do the same. There is consensus in Israel that Hamas must be disarmed, but what about the future of Israel? Netanyahu, Gantz, Eisenkot and other government members: Tell us immediately what the long-term goals of this war are, so we know what we are risking and perhaps sacrificing our lives for.

TITLE: Early farmers spreading out of Anatolia explain mystery of Neanderthal DNA in east Asians
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-19T10:47:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/archaeology/2023-10-19/ty-article/early-farmers-spreading-out-of-anatolia-explain-mystery-of-neanderthal-dna-in-east-asians/0000018b-46c8-d614-abcf-eefb01cb0000

We all carry genes from other human species, to differing degrees. We know that now. But there are incongruities. One anomaly is that today’s East Asians have 8 to 24 percent more Neanderthal ancestry than West Europeans. That is puzzling because the Neanderthals’ stamping ground was southwestern and central Eurasia, and the Middle East. They never reached eastern Asia, insofar as is known.
Various ideas have been propounded to explain this, including the vagaries of Darwinian natural section. Now a new hypothesis based on analysis of a genomic database of humans from 40,000 years ago to date was published Wednesday in Science Advances.
Hunter-gatherers in Europe indeed had more Neanderthal DNA than their East Asian counterparts until the Neolithic, the authors explain. That is as one would expect.
But about 10,000 years ago, early farmers with lower levels of Neanderthal ancestry began to spread out of Anatolia (aka Turkish Anadolu) into Europe. They mixed with the local hunter-gatherers, who had high Neanderthal ancestry. The result was dilution of the Neanderthal signal in their progeny, propose Claudio Quilodrán, Jérémy Rio, Alexandros Tsoupas and Mathias Currat of Switzerland’s University of Geneva.
Note that even if 8 to 24 percent sounds like a lot, the differences are not huge. “Our results could give the false impression that some populations have almost no Neanderthal DNA and others have a lot,” Currat says in a Zoom interview. “People in Eurasia nowadays have around 2 percent Neanderthal on average.”
So an 8-24 percent difference between Europe and East Asia translates to maybe 1.8 percent on the European end and 2.2 percent on the Asian end, to give an idea, he says. Yet these little differences are very telling.
The new study was able to spot subtle differences in Neanderthal contribution to humans by location and time going back 40,000 years thanks to the database put together by geneticist Prof. David Reich of Harvard and others, Currat adds.
How today’s Asians have any Neanderthal DNA in the first place
If Neanderthals never reached eastern Asia, why do eastern Asians have any Neanderthal DNA at all? Because they too descend from people who exited Africa via the Middle East around 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. We all have some Neanderthal DNA because all non-Africans today descend from people who exited Africa through the Middle East, which was thronged with Neanderthals. Thus, the wave of modern humans who successfully colonized Eurasia reached it with Neanderthal DNA inside.
Note that this wasn’t the first meeting of the two species. Homo sapiens seems to have been leaving Africa for at least 200,000 years. But early sapiens groups reaching Europe went extinct. (Before going extinct they mated with Neanderthals. We know this because Neanderthals in Siberia, Croatia and Spain from 100,000 years ago turned out to have Homo sapiens genetic sequences. These early meetings however weren’t the source of Neanderthal DNA in our genomes because these humans weren’t our ancestors – they died out.)
So: Meetings between Homo sapiens who were our ancestors and Neanderthals apparently began in the Middle East. Then, as humans reached Europe and forayed further and further northwest, they met more Neanderthals and mixed with them too, Quilodrán explains.
The further north into Europe the humans went, the more Neanderthals they encountered.
Meanwhile, more and more humans would continue to come out of Africa with little to no Neanderthal DNA, going into southern Europe. Thus, a gradient was created in prehistoric Europe: the humans in the north had more Neanderthal DNA than humans in southern Europe, the team discovered.
Now, regarding the west versus east: The team found that ancient European humans 40,000 years ago and 30,000 years ago and 20,000 years ago had more Neanderthal DNA than the Asian humans – exactly as one would expect, because as the humans went into eastern Asia, they did not encounter more Neanderthals.
So how did today’s western Europeans wind up with less Neanderthal DNA than today’s East Asians? Because about 10,000 years ago, early farmers from what is today Turkey began to spread to Europe.
Meanwhile, in Anatolia
A previous hypothesis to explain the Asian anomaly is based on natural selection: that some human groups were positively affected by the Neanderthal contribution and others were negatively affected, Quilodrán explains. This may be so, but the team’s research tested a different hypothesis: that the degree of Neanderthal ancestry in various populations today was affected by human migrations.
To explore this hypothesis, the team analyzed Neanderthal ancestry in 4,465 published human genomes from across Eurasia from about 40,000 years ago to today. With that great database, they could show the gradient in Neanderthal ancestry from north to south.
In the Neolithic, the levels of Neanderthal ancestry in the south were low. And when the early farmers from Anatolia in the south began to migrate massively into western Europe, they mixed with the local hunter-gatherers and diluted the Neanderthal ancestry there.
What happened in Asia remains to be investigated, but the situation is more complex than in Europe and much less data is available, the researchers tell Haaretz. But meanwhile we find dilution of the Neanderthal signal in Europe but not in Asia. QED.
“This second range expansion [out of Anatolia] is essential for explaining the pattern currently observed of lower [Neanderthal] ancestry in western Europe than in East Asia,” the team concludes.
Not the Denisovans
Neanderthals and Homo sapiens weren’t the only human species roaming Eurasia. Another was the Denisovans – a sister species to Neanderthals, who lived at the same time. While the Neanderthals dwelled in western Europe, the Denisovans were in the east.
There are areas where both species overlapped, such as Siberia. Also, we now know that modern humans interbred with Denisovans too.
Asked if the Neanderthal DNA in East Asians could actually be Denisovan DNA, the researchers say not, pointing at other studies.
“The observation of the Neanderthal DNA in the East Asians seems robust as it has been found several times with different methods, even if the exact amount of Neanderthal ancestry higher in current East Asians is still debated,” Currat says (hence the range of 8 to 24 percent).
How much Neanderthal DNA did the early farmers in Anatolia have? Around 2 percent, which is about the same as you probably have, dear reader. But in any case, it was “slightly less” than European hunter-gatherers of the same period, Currat says.
“In short, before the start of the Neolithic period [10,000 years ago], hunter-gatherers in Anatolia had slightly lower Neanderthal ancestry than hunter-gatherers in Europe, because they were closer to the source of the out-of-Africa expansion, according to our hypothesis. Then hunter-gatherers of Anatolia became farmers and their descendants migrated to Europe, contributing to decrease the amount of Neanderthal ancestry in Europe.”
And so today, Europeans have about 1.8 to 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry shaped by the migration of early farmers from Anatolia, who arose from hunter-gatherers in Anatolia who had relatively less Neanderthal DNA. And East Asians, undiluted, have a little more.

TITLE: Israel's dead: The names of those killed in Hamas attacks, massacres and the Israel-Hamas war
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-19T12:00:00+03:00
