TITLE: 150,000 missiles aimed at Israel: How far does Hezbollah's deadly arsenal reach
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-23T10:18:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/security-aviation/2023-10-23/ty-article-magazine/150-000-rockets-and-missiles-the-weapons-israel-would-encounter-in-a-war-with-hezbollah/0000018b-573d-d2b2-addf-777df6210000

"We are now at the point where Hezbollah has far more rockets and missiles than most governments in the world," said the U.S. defense secretary in a joint press conference with his Israeli counterpart. It was in 2010 that Robert Gates gave his grave assessment alongside Ehud Barak. Since then, Hezbollah has only gotten stronger.
The Lebanese terrorist organization has immensely expanded and upgraded its stockpile of rockets and various weapons systems, with the help of an enthusiastic Iran and the experience the group gained when helping to rescue Bashar al-Assad's rule in the Syrian Civil War.
According to the latest public estimates, Hezbollah has around 150,000 rockets and missiles, most with a range of a few dozen kilometers. Various reports, however, say a substantial number can reach targets located hundreds of kilometers from Lebanon.
Hezbollah is the most heavily armed non-state actor in the world, concluded researchers from the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington in an extensive 2018 report on the lethal arsenal stationed just north of Israel. The group holds a large and diverse reserve of "dumb" rocket artillery alongside ballistic, anti-air, anti-tank, and anti-ship missiles, the report found.
In a conversation with Haaretz this week, Shaan Shaikh, one of the study’s authors, warned that Hezbollah's intervention in Syria “raises concerns about its acquisition of more sophisticated standoff and precision-guided missiles, whether from Syria, Iran, or Russia.” Standoff missiles are long-range systems that can be fired from far enough away that the launchers remain protected.
According to an article recently published by the Institute for National Security Studies, Hezbollah has about 40,000 short-range Grad-type rockets; 80,000 Fajr-3 and Fajr-5, Khaibar, and Ra'ad medium-long-range rockets; and 30,000 long-range Zelzal rockets and Fateh-110 (M600) missiles. According to the article, Hezbollah has also received a limited number of Scud-type missiles from Syria. Several hundred Fateh-110 missiles, which carry around 500 kilograms (1,100 pounds), “are equipped with precise GPS-based navigation mechanisms and have considerable accuracy and destructive potential," according to the report.
The military and Defense Ministry estimate that Hezbollah may fire several thousand rockets on the first few days of war and continue with 1,500 a day for the rest. During the Second Lebanon War in 2006, Hezbollah fired approximately 200 rockets a day.
In recent years, the group has devoted most of its efforts to its "precision project," a concentrated attempt to add guiding systems to its unguided rockets. The goal is to transform them from indiscriminate weapons to ones that are able not just to strike terror in an enemy population but also directly hit strategic targets such as headquarters, military bases, power stations, and areas with troop concentrations.
Alongside Hezbollah's immense artillery arsenal, the organization has a large stock of anti-aircraft missiles, including shoulder-fired ones to down helicopters and low-altitude aircraft. Shoulder-fired missiles leave no signature revealing the location of those launching them, who can disappear quickly. Hezbollah also has heavy anti-air systems, including surface-to-air missiles and launchers, that can hit aerial targets at a range of up to 50 kilometers (31 miles) at a height of up to 24 kilometers.
One of the most serious blows the IDF suffered during the Second Lebanon War was the damage wreaked by Hezbollah's extensive anti-tank units, particularly by their Russian-developed Kornet guided. Like the American Javelin, the Kornet can hit tanks from above, where the armor is relatively thin.
Since 2011, Israel has equipped its Armored Corps' tanks with a Trophy protective system that identifies and intercepts anti-tank missile launches. In 2014, the Trophy system successfully intercepted Kornet missiles. It hasn’t made the tanks indestructible in the face of the missiles, but it has improved the survivability of the tank and the crew inside it.
Besides Hezbollah's formidable missile arsenal, the organization has been developing its own air force for over 20 years based on drones in a variety of sizes and roles, some manufactured in Iran and some locally. These drones can carry weapons or be fitted with heavy warheads to function as suicide drones. The Alma Research and Education Center estimates that the organization has about 2,000 drones of diverse types, including civilian drones that have been repurposed to carry weapons.
Hezbollah also has a commando unit, the Radwan Force, which is supposed to be the spearhead in a potential war with Israel and may try to capture several towns and villages along the border in a manner similar to Hamas' attack in southern Israel two weeks ago. The force consists of some 2,500 personnel who train in Lebanon and Iran, including in paragliding and infiltration by sea. Many of them have experience from the Syrian Civil War.
In 2018, the IDF uncovered tunnels under the northern border intended to let Hezbollah infiltrate Israeli towns unhindered. October 7, 2023, proved that tunnels are only one of the possible methods of invading Israel.

TITLE: Cutting-edge surgical lasers deliver outstanding results
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-23T12:45:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/haaretz-labels/medica/2023-10-23/ty-article-labels/.premium/cutting-edge-surgical-lasers-deliver-outstanding-results/0000018b-5be0-d2b2-addf-7ff89a1c0000

Among many doctors who perform Endovenous Laser Ablation (EVLA) – a common procedure for treating varicose veins – neoLaser has become synonymous with superior, high-quality performance, and it is rapidly becoming the platform of choice in clinics around the world. This is a field where quality is of utmost importance. During these invasive procedures, vascular surgeons use infrared lasers to seal off varicose veins, typically in patients’ legs, in order to reroute the blood flow to healthy veins.
Most laser systems offer a power output precision rate of around 80%, whereas neoLaser’s platform enables a precision rate of 95% – which is a very substantial improvement. “It used to be that for every 100 patients there could be 5-6 failures. Now there are much fewer, because neoLaser ensures that it’s done right,” says Gil Shapira, the company’s Founder, President and CEO.
Not surprisingly, as soon as it was introduced eight years ago, neoLaser was warmly welcomed by doctors who perform EVLA. The company initially focused on Germany and within just one year, neoLaser captured a 10% share of that quality-driven market. The brand soon became entrenched throughout Europe, and today it is a global leader, with distributors in 40 countries throughout North and South America, Asia, and Australia, in addition to Europe.
Profitable from the start
NeoLaser is a rare bird: it is an Israeli start-up that was profitable from a very early stage. Gil Shapira founded the family-owned company in 2012. By then, he had over 20 years of experience in the surgical laser and technology industry as an engineer, product developer and manager. He previously served as an officer in the Israeli Air Force, where he managed advanced technology projects and headed product development at OmniGuide, an MIT medical device spin-off. Shapira holds an M.Sc in Electrical Engineering from Tel Aviv University and an MBA from MIT’s Sloan School of Management.
“We started out ten years ago and were profitable from a very early stage. Our vision was to create a super high-quality product that fits into existing markets. We funded the first stages ourselves and bootstrapped the operation. Revenues grew organically with a CAGR of over 40% since the launch of sales,” the CEO and Founder reveals. All of the R&D and manufacturing for the EVLA system takes place in neoLaser’s facilities in Caesarea, Israel.
The secret to neoLaser’s success lies in its meticulous design. The company’s engineers and designers insist on using only the highest quality materials and components, including full aluminum housing and the most advanced optical technologies. “From the beginning, we were committed to providing the highest quality platform and we wanted it to be extremely reliable and easy to operate,” says Shapira. For example, from day one neoLaser used fused caps for securing the fibers’ glass caps, rather than using glue to connect them – as do many other brands – since fusing is much safer and more stable.
NeoLaser’s EVLA system is also considerably smaller and more elegant than other models. Weighing just 3.5 kgs., it doesn’t take up much space and is easy to ship and transport. “We are proud of our design excellence, both externally and internally,” notes Shapira. Another advantage: it has a user-friendly interface so that doctors don’t require any special training; they simply need to adjust their settings.
Groundbreaking treatments
In recent years, neoLaser also launched a series of state-of-the-art laser systems for proctological procedures. Unlike the EVLA market, where lasers have long been the leading technology, lasers were not previously used for treating proctological conditions such as mid- to high-grade hemorrhoids. Traditionally, the prevailing approach for patients in this category was to subject them to full-out surgery involving a long and painful recuperation process, or other techniques with high recurrence rates. NeoLaser’s laser system for hemorrhoids is revolutionary in that it makes it possible to treat patients with Grade 3 (medium-high grade) hemorrhoids in a safe and efficient manner that is much less painful and entails almost no downtime with excellent symptom resolution.
In the short time since its launch in this market, neoLaser has become a leader all over the world, with sales of the device doubling last year. “This product is the largest growth engine for us. Its success has been phenomenal,” confirms Shapira. Since this is a completely new type of treatment, doctors need to be educated and trained. Therefore, neoLaser offers courses and webinars for professionals, and operates training centers in different regions around the world.
The company has also introduced other groundbreaking products for proctologists: laser probes to treat pilonidal sinuses as well as anal fistulas. A pilonidal sinus is a small cavity above the buttocks area that becomes inflamed, while an anal fistula is an abnormal channel between the inside of the anus and the outside skin around the anus. Although these conditions are less common than hemorrhoids, their usual surgical treatment techniques often entail either long down times or high risks of serious long-term complications. Using lasers rather than aggressive surgery, neoLaser has devised a treatment that mitigates these horrible side effects, is much less painful, and involves a substantially shorter recuperation time. With products that have such obvious benefits, the sky is clearly the limit for neoLaser.

TITLE: Two Israeli women, Yocheved Lifshitz and Nurit Cooper, released from Hamas captivity
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-23T12:52:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-23/ty-article-live/world-leaders-tell-israel-to-adhere-to-international-law-gaza-running-out-of-fuel/0000018b-5a5d-d00f-a9bf-7a5da4e10000

Updates
Continue reading updates on the day 18 liveblog
Live updates here have ended. To continue reading live updates from day 18, click here.
Families of Israeli hostages to protest at UN on Tuesday
A delegation of the families of hostages held captive by Hamas will be at the United Nations at the same time as U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken, who will travel to New York City tomorrow to participate in a United Nations Security Council Ministerial on the situation in the Middle East.
The families will hold demonstrations at the UN, as well as meeting with UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, New York City Mayor Eric Adams and U.S. Jewish leaders.
Blinken meets Jewish, Arab-American and Palestinian-American leaders
U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken held separate meetings with Jewish community leaders, as well as representatives of the Arab-American and Palestinian-American communities.
"In both discussions, the Secretary condemned Hamas’ horrific terrorist attacks against Israel, reaffirmed the United States’ ironclad commitment to Israel’s security, outlined his recent engagements and travel to the Middle East, and described the United States’ efforts to see to it that all civilians are protected and to prevent the widening of the conflict. He stressed that no civilian life is worth more than another — whether Christian, Jewish, or Muslim – and emphasized ongoing U.S. efforts to facilitate a steady flow of humanitarian assistance to civilians in Gaza, as we work with partners across the region to secure the release of additional hostages," the State Department said.
The meetings come as the Biden administration's Israel policy comes under increasing scrutiny from the Arab community, as well as critics within the State Department.
Biden reaffirms support for Israel, underscores need to sustain a flow of humanitarian aid into Gaza
U.S. President Joe Biden spoke to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu early Tuesday morning, reaffirming “his commitment to ongoing efforts to secure the release of all the remaining hostages taken by Hamas – including Americans – and to provide for safe passage for U.S. citizens and other civilians in Gaza,” according to a readout of the conversation provided by the White House.
Biden also “underscored the need to sustain a continuous flow of urgently needed humanitarian assistance into Gaza.”
The two leaders agreed to speak again in the coming days, according to the White House.
China will do utmost to contribute to Palestinian-Israeli reconciliation, state media says
China will do its utmost when it comes to contributing to Palestinian-Israeli reconciliation, its foreign minister told his Israel counterpart in a phone call on Monday, according to Chinese state media.
China will also firmly support any resolution as long as it is conducive to peace, minister Wang Yi said, calling the conflict a "major choice between war and peace", state media said on Tuesday.
Wang also called for Israel to take effective measures to protect the safety of Chinese citizens and institutions there, adding that "all countries have the right to self-defense, but they should abide by international humanitarian law and protect the safety of civilians."
France’s Macron to visit Israel, Ramallah on Tuesday
French President Emmanuel Macron will land in Israel on Tuesday morning for meetings with Israeli and Palestinian officials. He will be met at Ben-Gurion Airport by representatives of the French nationals killed in the fighting or being held captive by Hamas in the Gaza Strip.
Macron will meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog, as well as members of the Israeli war cabinet and opposition leaders, before travelling to Ramallah where he will meet with Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas.
U.S. welcomes release of hostages, calls for all to be set free
United States National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan said that the U.S. "welcomes today’s release of two Israeli citizens held hostage by Hamas. We continue to do everything possible to secure the release of all remaining hostages in Gaza," he added.
State Department spokesman Matthew Miller said that the United States is "very gratified" that the two Israeli women had been released.
"Well, obviously we're very gratified to see the release of these two hostages - Israeli citizens - which comes on top of the release on Friday have to American citizens really since the immediate aftermath of the attack on Israel on October 7," Miller said during an appearance on MSNBC on Monday.
Israel will not hold off on ground offensive over hostages, minister tells Bild
Israel will not hold off on a possible ground invasion of Gaza over the issue of captives being held there, Israel's energy minister told German tabloid newspaper Bild. In an interview published on Tuesday, energy minister Israel Katz said everything would be done to bring the hostages home. "But that cannot hinder our actions including the ground offensive, if we decide on it," he was quoted as saying.
"Hamas wants us to deal with the captives and wants the military to not go in to eliminate their infrastructure. That will not happen," Katz added.

TITLE: Hostage's mother: 'Israel has to be very careful about causing harm that we can't undo'
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-24T01:14:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/podcasts/2023-10-24/ty-article-podcast/anderson-cooper-said-i-have-a-video-of-your-kidnapped-son/0000018b-5e1a-d8e2-a1eb-ff1e67b50000

The "alternative universe" Rachel Goldberg has been living in since her son Hersh Goldberg-Polin, 23, a dual U.S.-Israeli citizen, was kidnapped by Hamas, has included non-stop interviews with the media. Rachel and her husband Jonathan have appeared on the cover of TIME Magazine and spoke to "any outlet that would talk" to them, to advocate for humanitarian treatment and expedited release of their son and over 220 hostages being held captive in Gaza.
An appearance on CNN last week, she recounts to Haaretz Weekly host Allison Kaplan Sommer, took an unexpected turn when anchor Anderson Cooper – who is making a documentary about the Supernova music festival massacre - put together her account of witnesses saying her son's arm had been severed, and something he had seen while in the field reporting on the deadly attack.
"At the end of the interview, Anderson Cooper said: have you guys seen any video of Hersh? We said no - and we've had a friend who has been trying - searching through all the horrible videos that are out there. And then Anderson said, 'I have a video of your son.'"
The worried family, she said, was glad, on one hand, to see the video show that their son had the strength to walk and lift himself up by one arm into the kidnappers' truck.
"But then he turns, you see this bloody stump, and it takes your breath away," she said.
Goldberg, who details on the podcast the way her family and its team of supporters had been able to piece together what had happened to Hersh, said she had been "thrilled" at the news of the release of American hostages Judith and Natalie Raanan, who she noted, were, like their family, from Chicago.
"I'm hopeful that the powers that made that happen, will continue to see it through," Goldberg said.
As to how the continuing efforts to release the hostages will play out, Goldberg hopes that even though "you have people in the street who have gone through complete and utter trauma and are thirsty for an aggressive response… the government is using every ounce of thoughtfulness and wisdom when making its plan."
"There are hundreds of innocent hostages, and I'll also mention there are hundreds of thousands of innocent Gazans who are also trapped there," she says. "We have to be very careful about not causing harm that we can't undo, and I think there is time to plan this out in a way that our soldiers are not embroiled in a situation that will bring us so much more pain, danger and loss of life."

Florida's DeSantis bans pro-Palestinian student group
Florida’s university system, working with Governor Ron DeSantis, ordered colleges on Tuesday to shut down a pro-Palestinian student organization, marking the first U.S. state to outlaw the group whose national leadership backed Hamas' attack on Israel.
The State University System of Florida said chapters of Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP) had to be dismantled as part of a "crack down" in the Republican-led state on campus demonstrations that provide "harmful support for terrorist groups."
"Based on the National SJP’s support of terrorism, in consultation with Governor DeSantis, the student chapters must be deactivated," the system's Chancellor Ray Rodrigues wrote in a memo to university leaders.
SJP is active in at least two Florida universities, Rodrigues said.
The University of North Florida in Jacksonville and Florida State University in Tallahassee have SJP chapters, based on Instagram sites. The National SJP did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The commander of the IDF’s 13th Golani Brigade, Lt. Col. Tomer Greenbaum, said Tuesday that his troops are preparing for a ground invasion of the Gaza Strip. “This time,” he added, “we will have the element of surprise. We will come with a concentrated force, with all of the advanced capabilities and high standard of the Brigade – and we will be victorious.”
U.S. has 'high confidence' Palestinian rocket caused Gaza hospital blast
U.S. intelligence officials have "high confidence" that an explosion at a Gaza hospital last week was caused by a Palestinian rocket that broke up mid-flight, and not by Israel, a U.S. official said on Tuesday.
The Hamas-run Gaza health ministry said 471 people were killed in the blast at Al-Ahli al-Arabi Hospital last week. Palestinians and Arab states said an Israeli air strike hit the hospital.
Israel said the blast was caused by a failed rocket launch by Islamic Jihad, which has denied responsibility.
U.S. President Biden said a day after the incident, while visiting Tel Aviv, that the explosion appeared to be the result of an errant rocket fired by a "terrorist group", echoing Israel's view.
U.S. media reported the U.S. intelligence assessment on Tuesday, citing a briefing with reporters. The U.S. official declined to be named as the information remained confidential.
The officials said there was still uncertainty around the death toll and the number of injuries, the New York Times reported. The officials said there was little damage to the hospital and the structure did not collapse, it reported.
The intelligence assessment was based on Israeli intercepts of Palestinian groups, publicly available video, communications intercepts provided by the Israelis and images of the blast and the aftermath, the officials told the newspaper.
An unclassified U.S. intelligence report seen by Reuters two days after the blast estimated the death toll was "probably at the low end of the 100 to 300 spectrum" but added that the assessment may evolve.
Israeli military carries out a drone strike in Jenin during clashes with armed Palestinians
The IDF said early Wednesday that it carried out a drone strike against armed Palestinians in the Jenin refugee camp during an arrest operation.
According to a statement, Palestinians opened fire and threw explosive devices at Israeli forces who had arrested two terror suspects in area. The military said a drone was called in to neutralize the threat. The IDF added that there were no Israeli causalities.
The Palestinian Red Crescent ambulance service said two Palestinians were killed, with others injured, some of them critically. Islamic Jihad said that one of its members, Mahmoud al-Fayad, 20, was killed in the drone strike.

Australia deploys more aircraft, personnel to Middle East
Australia said on Wednesday it had deployed two more military aircraft and a "significant number" of defense personnel to the Middle East to help support its citizens there if the ongoing war between Israel and militant group Hamas escalates.
Australia sent a Boeing C-17 aircraft and an air refueler plane that has the capacity to carry passengers, taking the total to three, Defence Minister Richard Marles said.
He did not disclose the total number of personnel deployed and where the aircraft would be based due to security reasons but said they would not be based in Israel.
"It is a significant number of personnel, though, and they're there to support the aircraft and to support what that aircraft might ultimately have to do," Marles told Channel Nine.
"All of this is a contingency and the purpose of it is to be supporting Australian populations that are in the Middle East ... this is a very volatile situation and we just don't absolutely know which way it goes from here."
Since the conflict began, the Australian government has conducted repatriation flights for citizens stranded in Israel. It has been trying to rescue 79 Australians from the Israeli-besieged Gaza Strip and 51 from the West Bank.
Australians in Gaza should try to move toward the Rafah border crossing with Egypt, the main entry and exit point to Gaza that does not lead to Israel, Marles said.

TITLE: Paleontologists deduce what a trilobite ate for lunch 465 million years ago
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-24T18:16:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/science/2023-10-24/ty-article/paleontologists-deduce-what-a-trilobite-ate-for-lunch-465-million-years-ago/0000018b-620c-ddfd-a59f-e3ec3a860000

About 465 million years ago, a trilobite died. It was one of the many trilobites who thronged the Cambrian seas. But this one was uniquely preserved for eternity with its lunch inside, to the delight of paleontologists whose evolution would begin 465 million years later.
Yes, our whole species falls within the margin of error of this little animal. The discovery of the exquisitely preserved arthropod with its meal in its gut was reported in Nature in September.
Countless trilobite fossils have been found to date, some tiny little things and some as long as your arm. They’re easy to find on eBay and Amazon. Indeed, “trilobites are among the most iconic of fossils,” begins the paper by paleontologist Petr Kraft of Charles University in Prague and colleagues.
These segmented arthropods survived for around 270 million years, diversifying madly to occupy multiple oceanic niches and dominating the seafloors until their extinction with most of life on Earth in the Permian 252 million years ago. Paleontologists have counted over 20,000 species of trilobite, including some very tiny ones and giants 72 centimeters (28 inches) in length.
But this one, found in the Czech Republic, is the first among the thousands upon thousands of trilobite fossils found to date to shed concrete light on the feeding habits and lifestyle of the creatures.
The hyena of the Permian
Paleontologists may have counted thousands 20,000 trilobite species during their 270-million-year reign from the early Cambrian to the end of the Permian, but what they ate had remained a mystery. It still is – but in the case of one specific individual, Bohemolichas incola, Kraft and his colleagues found its gut packed full of broken shells from sea creatures.
Which sea creatures? The likes of clams and cone shells, conch, extinct echinoderms (surviving echinoderms include sea urchins and starfish), and mainly ostracods – sometimes known as “seed shrimp.”
The shell fragments are so well preserved that the paleontologists even venture to name some specific species, such as Conchoprimitia osekensis.
Interestingly, predatory arthropods tend to be specific in their prey choices but our trilobite was not, the researchers say. Incola was polyphagous: it chose its meals based on size and shell resistance, not species. And that non-selectivity suggests to the authors that it was not a hunter like a lion but primarily a scavenger like a hyena.
Our trilobite is believed to have crushed their shells using its feet, employing the spines on their many legs to shred the prey.
A separate study examined whether this was even possible based on the extant horseshoe crab, a living fossil that arose at least 450 million years ago. It is, they concluded. “Redlichia rex ... spanning 25 centimeters and armed with bulky legs, was effectively built like a tank,” and therefore was probably highly capable of shell-crushing destruction, that study wrote. Incola was more likely a “light crusher,” the new paper suggests; a chance feeder that happily ate the small animals in its path, alive or dead.
It also had quite the appetite, the paleontologists deduce: its gut was tightly packed with the shell fragments, indicating high feeding intensity.
So what have we? The incola can be considered as a light crusher and chance feeder “hoovering up dead or living animals that were either easily disintegrated or small enough to be swallowed whole,” the authors describe.
How surprising is this? Trilobites had been postulated to be carnivorous, but that could only be inferred. Now we have a trilobite with its prey, and it seems to have both hunted and scavenged. Which is relatable because that is exactly what we humans do.
And after it died, our incola suffered the same fate, the paleontologists found. Somebody scavenged its body – but, fortunately for us, they went for its soft tissues and left its gut alone. We know this because, the paleontologists explain, the fossil bears the marks of other scavengers who burrowed into the body but didn’t invade the gut. Why not? They may have been deterred by the noxious environment of the trilobite’s digestion.

DATE: 2023-10-24T18:21:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-24/ty-article-magazine/i-dont-have-time-to-let-this-pain-get-inside-my-head-i-cant-be-defeated/0000018b-61d3-d473-a5fb-65db97b00000

A blue sign opposite Ayelet Svatitzky’s house on Kibbutz Yagur in northern Israel tells the story of an old guard post whose remains can be seen poking out from inside the thick foliage.
During the Arab Revolt in the 1930s, the post was used as protection against the Arab gangs that were firing down from Mount Carmel onto the kibbutz located on its slopes. Ayelet also talks about the ingenious hiding places where kibbutz members would conceal weapons, and which British Mandatory forces raided during the 1946 military operation known as Black Sabbath.
That incident was a formative event in the history of the kibbutz, with many of its members arrested for alleged anti-British activities.
On the new Black Sabbath of October 7, it was actually relatively quiet on Kibbutz Yagur. However, on the kibbutz where Ayelet was born – Nirim, on the Gaza border – a massacre took place.
Her older brother, Roi Popplewell, 54, was murdered, while her 79-year-old mother, Channah Peri, and brother Nadav Popplewell, 51, were abducted and are apparently being held by Hamas in Gaza.
That morning, Ayelet woke at about 8 A.M. and heard her partner, Eyal, talking on the phone in an unusual manner. “He told me, ‘Something bad is happening in the south, call your mother,’” she recounts.
“I took the phone and realized that the WhatsApp group of members of my class on the kibbutz – which actually means all of my childhood friends – was blowing up. One of them lives in Nirim; others live in moshavim in the area but have parents in Nirim. And they’re saying there’s been a missile attack and infiltration of terrorists on the kibbutz. I called my mother in hysterics and told her: ‘There are missiles, go into the safe room and lock yourself inside.’
“I don’t have a safe room here, so I didn’t know that they’re not designed with doors that lock. They’re designed to protect you from missile attacks, not terrorists. She told me that the house wasn’t locked. We didn’t have time to exchange another sentence before I heard a man’s voice talking to her in English with a heavy Arabic accent.
“I didn’t think twice. I interrupted our conversation and called my brother Nadav, who lives next door, 10 meters [about 33 feet] from her. I also told him: lock the safe room, don’t dare go out; I don’t know what’s happening in mom’s house. I didn’t want to tell him what I knew was happening in her house. Before I managed to finish the sentence, I heard the same voices with an Arabic accent in his house as well.”
British-Israeli Ayelet rushed to call an acquaintance at the kibbutz, which has a population of 400, and was able to tell her what she had just heard. The woman promised to send the information to the kibbutz security team, but then their conversation was cut off. By this point, the security team was already in the midst of a battle against terrorists in a different part of the kibbutz.
“The security teams were always told: the army is behind you. Even if it isn’t with you inside the kibbutz – hold on for 20 minutes, hold on for half an hour, until the army arrives. Nobody ever imagined an infiltration of dozens of terrorists into each community, along the entire border.
“But the army didn’t arrive. The area fell, communications were faltering. And yet can I say that’s a good-enough explanation for why in the State of Israel, which can be traversed from end to end in five hours, the army didn’t arrive for so many hours? It isn’t. It’s not as though they had to bring the forces from Los Angeles.”
Several minutes after she told her kibbutz acquaintance that terrorists had entered the homes of both her mother and brother, Ayelet received two pictures on WhatsApp showing Channah and Nadav sitting in the living room of her mother’s house. An armed terrorist was standing behind them and, in the corner of the picture, an unidentified figure was holding a Kalashnikov rifle. Below was a caption in English: “Hamas.”
“It’s not certain that they knew there was a family connection when they brought my brother from his house to hers,” she says. “It’s possible that they only understood the family connection when they were together. They posted another picture from the same series on my mother’s Facebook Stories. All that happened between 8:15 and 8:30 A.M., something like that.”
In the picture you see Ayelet’s mother sitting in a nightgown covered with a blanket, a glass of water in her hand. Nadav is sitting on a nearby sofa, barefoot. Both mother and son are diabetic and need medication for their condition.
‘We had no idea’
The last word Ayelet Svatitzky received about the fate of her mother and brother came from a neighbor who saw them being led out of Channah’s house, walking on their own two feet and looking healthy. But she only received this news two days after the attack. “After seeing the pictures, for several hours I was sure that they’d been killed,” she recounts. “I wasn’t in contact with my older brother [Roi] during all those hours because we’re never in contact during an incident, only when it’s over.
“Only when they started talking in the media about the fact that there are hostages did I start to think that maybe this is what happened to them. Because otherwise, why should Hamas take a picture of them and send me ‘a sign of life’? But during the first four hours, I thought they’d been murdered. We sat here outside, my husband and I – we hadn’t told the children anything at this point; I didn’t want them to try to make contact with them.
“The only thing that interested me during those first four hours, when I thought [Channah and Nadav] were dead, was that my friends and their families should be taken away from there, so that nobody else would go through what I was going through. We had no idea how many people were going to have that experience.”
When the army finally arrived at Nirim and started to evacuate the residents from their homes, they contacted Ayelet to tell her they hadn’t found her mother or brother. Nor did they find Roi, who lived in a different part of the kibbutz, at home. “I thought that maybe he went out early to feed the cats in the fields – because that’s where he worked – and maybe he was hiding there, or they took him to Gaza too.”
On the Sunday, she went to submit a missing persons report for her two brothers and mother, and to give DNA samples. However, when she arrived at the police station, she received a phone call from a resident at the kibbutz. They informed her that Roi’s body had been found on the lawn behind his house.
Ayelet herself has been told very little by the authorities. “I only know that they found him shot, and I didn’t ask for more details. It’s not relevant to me. I don’t need pictures in my head, nor do I watch all the Hamas video clips [of the massacre] that are being posted now. I can’t let anything in that might cause me to go into shock, to affect my functioning. I’m on a mission at the moment. I can’t do anything about my slain brother. We know for sure that he was murdered and the official identification will arrive. At least I know – that’s more than others have. Not knowing is worse than my situation.”
A happy divorce
Roi, Nadav and Ayelet were all born on Kibbutz Nirim. Channah had immigrated to Israel from South Africa when she was in her twenties, for Zionistic reasons. When she came to the kibbutz to visit a friend who had made aliyah with her, she met a new immigrant from England and they married soon after. Channah ran the kibbutz sewing workshop for a while, as well as the grocery store. The siblings’ father worked in the cowshed but died 18 years ago. The couple divorced when Ayelet was 13.
The divorce was actually what made them good friends, Ayelet explains. “It was very important to my mother for my father to have a partner. So she registered him for the singles group in the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel, because my father loved to hike. And he really did meet a wonderful partner, Yehudit, and they were together for several years. My parents became very good friends; we were lucky in that sense. They realized that it hadn’t worked out for them as a couple and that enabled us to build a much more stable, strong and good family unit after they separated.
“One of the best things that happened to me was my parents divorcing. Suddenly, the stress of a relationship that didn’t work was gone and each of them could flourish as a person. I grew up in the cowshed. The smell of cow dung is the smell of home for me. It makes no difference how many years I’ve been living at Yagur. Yagur is home for me, but Nirim will also always be my home. One doesn’t cancel out the other.”
Since the birth of Ayelet’s three children – her brothers have no children – Channah has proved to be a natural grandmother.
“She’s the most wonderful grandmother you could ask for,” Ayelet relays. “She comes here once a month and sleeps here with my brother Nadav; we eat our Friday night meal together and play board games. He’s a wonderful uncle and she’s an outstanding grandmother. She taught my daughter to knit.”
After retiring a few years ago, Channah enjoyed a quiet and peaceful life in Nirim, as did the two brothers.
“She enjoyed her Tai Chi and Qigong; on Fridays they travel to Sderot or Ofakim to shop for Shabbat. Nadav works in Sderot, he’s a computer person. He loves science fiction, plays bridge. And my mother – in the past year we struggled a little with the eyesight in one of her eyes and her balance wasn’t great, so my brothers would come cook for her or eat supper with her. She had a good, quiet and satisfying life. Roi had a small and limited group of wonderful people as friends. He raised a street cat that adopted him. A real kibbutznik. He’d sit in the evening with his Goldstar beer, relaxed, in a cowboy hat. He loved working in the garden.”
How did they feel about the threats from Gaza?
“When there were serious incidents that forced them to evacuate, they’d come to me. And I always thought, as someone observing from a distance, that it wasn’t normal. What kind of expression is a ‘drizzle of rockets’ anyway? It’s not rain; it’s missiles. I couldn’t understand how that was the norm. They always said it was 95 percent paradise and 5 percent hell. And they always accepted the fact that they’re able to live with the ‘5 percent hell’ for the ‘95 percent paradise.’ But this time, 100 percent hell fell on us. It was their home. There was no chance they would leave.”
What makes you optimistic that they’re in Gaza?
“I don’t think about what’s happening there now; I put that aside. My mission is to bring them home. If I start thinking about whether or not they have their pills [for the diabetes], that will only defeat me. I don’t have the privilege of being defeated at this time. I’m active. I have to make sure that the list of their medications is in the hands of someone who can perhaps give it to someone who can provide them. I can’t cross the border fence and give them the pills, but I can post their pictures, tell their story.
“They’re there, and I don’t preoccupy myself with questions that won’t help me. If I start thinking at night about what the situation is there with the bombings, it will only defeat me. At the moment, we’re doing everything possible to bring them home. I’m very calm on that matter. I don’t have time to let this pain get inside my head. I can’t collapse. Afterward, we’ll allow that to come, to defeat us, to cause us pain, to crush us. It will come, for sure – after all, I lost a brother. But not now.”

TITLE: Netanyahu: I too will answer for Hamas attack; Biden: Two-state solution must be next
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-25T07:33:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-25/ty-article-live/israel-strikes-syrian-military-targets-biden-israel-will-decide-about-gaza-ground-op/0000018b-6479-d473-a5fb-64f9518e0000

Key Events
Updates
Biden and Netanyahu discuss Gaza, hostage release, and peace prospects
U.S. President Joe Biden and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu discussed spoke on Thursday and discussed the developments in Gaza, ongoing efforts to locate and secure the release of hostages, including American citizens believed to be held by Hamas. Additionally, they reviewed discussions concerning the safe passage of foreign nationals wishing to leave Gaza as soon as possible.
President Biden reiterated the United States' commitment to providing continuous humanitarian support to the civilian population in Gaza and expressed support for increasing this assistance in the near future. He emphasized Israel's right and responsibility to defend its citizens from terrorism while adhering to international humanitarian law.
Furthermore, President Biden stressed the importance of focusing on post-crisis efforts, including working towards a permanent peace between Israelis and Palestinians. He underscored that Hamas does not represent the Palestinian people or their legitimate aspirations.
The two leaders agreed to maintain regular consultations, both directly and through their respective national security teams.
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders calls for a humanitarian pause in Gaza amid pressure from former staffers to promote ceasefire
Sen. Bernie Sanders called for a humanitarian pause in Gaza, one day after hundreds of his former campaign staffers demanded he introduce a Senate resolution demanding a Gaza ceasefire.
"To my mind, a pause is essential for the protection of civilians as required by the laws of war, as well as for the provision of robust supplies of food, water, and medical aid to address the growing humanitarian catastrophe," he said.
"I have serious concerns about what this invasion and potential occupation of Gaza will mean, both in terms of the long-term security of Israel and the well-being of the Palestinian residents of Gaza. In Congress, as we consider a package including billions of dollars for Israel that could fund this invasion and occupation, we clearly need much more information about Israel’s long-term plans and goals, as well as the United States Government’s assessments of those prospects," Sanders added.
U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin speaks with Israeli counterpart Yoav Gallant
U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin spoke with Israeli counterpart Yoav Gallant, the latest in their near-daily phone calls following the October 7 Hamas attack.
U.S. Senator calls on Israel to allow fuel into Gaza
Sen. Chris Murphy — the top senator on the subcommittee dedicated to the Middle East — called on Israel to allow fuel to reach hospitals, desalination plants, and water pumping stations into Gaza – with all of the necessary protocols to prevent diversion into Hamas' hands.
"Emergency food supplies are dwindling and their entire aid distribution system needs fuel to operate," Murphy said after meeting with World Food Programme Executive Director Cindy McCain.
World Health Organization calls for 'immediate release, on humanitarian and health grounds, of all those abducted' by Hamas
The World Health Organization is "gravely concerned" about the condition of Israeli hostages captured by Hamas during the October 7 attack, calling for their immediate release and urgent access to each of them and delivery of medical care.
"There is an urgent need for the captors of the hostages to provide signs of life, proof of provision of health care and the immediate release, on humanitarian and health grounds, of all those abducted," said WHO Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
He added that many of the hostages — including children, women and the elderly — have pre-existing health conditions requiring urgent and sustained care and treatment.
"The mental health trauma that the abducted, and the families, are facing is acute and psychosocial support is of great importance," noted Ghebreyesus.
Major Muslim organization condemns Biden casting doubt on number of Gaza casualties
America's largest Muslim civil society organization condemned U.S. President Joe Biden's "shocking and dehumanizing" remarks casting doubt on the number of Palestinian casualties in Gaza, stating "it's the price of waging war."
"President Biden should watch some of these videos and ask himself if the crushed children being dragged out of the ruins of their family homes are a fabrication or an acceptable price of war. They are neither," said Council on American-Islamic Relations Executive Director Nihad Awad.
U.S. House overwhelmingly passed a resolution supporting Israel
The U.S. House overwhelmingly passed a resolution supporting Israel, in the first legislation passed since Mike Johnson became House speaker.
10 lawmakers (9 of whom were Democrats) voted no and six voted present (five of whom originally co-sponsored the resolution but have since called for a ceasefire).
The Democratic "no" votes: Reps. Cori Bush, Jamaal Bowman, Andre Carson, Al Green, Summer Lee, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, Delia Ramirez and Rashida Tlaib.
"Do not confuse my vote against this one-sided resolution with a lack of empathy for all those who are grieving. I voted against this resolution because it is a deeply incomplete and biased account of what is happening in Israel and Palestine, and what has been happening for decades," said Rep. Rashida Tlaib, the only Palestinian-American lawmaker in Congress.
"While the resolution rightly acknowledges and mourns the lives taken by Hamas, I cannot support a resolution that fails to acknowledge and mourn the lives of Palestinians taken by the Israeli military. The resolution also fails to acknowledge the Israeli government's military bombardment of Gaza, especially after Israeli officials openly admitted to implementing collective punishment of Palestinians in Gaza," said Rep. Ilhan Omar.
"Our position should be consistent in defending innocent lives. We must use diplomacy to secure the release of hostages, end the violence by negotiating a ceasefire, restore water, food, and fuel to Gaza, and work toward lasting peace," she added.
The Democratic "present" votes: Reps. Greg Casar, Joaquin Castro, Chuy Garcia, Pramila Jayapal, Nydia Velazquez and Ayanna Pressley.
The lone Republican no vote was from Rep. Thomas Massie.
Putin: Israel's conflict with Hamas 'could spill over far beyond the borders of the Middle East'
Oct 25 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin warned on Wednesday that Israel's conflict with Hamas could spread well beyond the Middle East and said it was wrong that innocent women, children and old people in Gaza were being punished for other people's crimes.
Putin, who made the comments in a Kremlin meeting with Russian religious leaders of different faiths, said bloodshed in the region had to stop. He said he told other world leaders in phone calls that if it did not, there was a risk of a much wider conflagration.
"Our task today, our main task, is to stop the bloodshed and violence," said Putin, according to a Kremlin transcript of the meeting.
"Otherwise, further escalation of the crisis is fraught with grave and extremely dangerous and destructive consequences. And not only for the Middle East region. It could spill over far beyond the borders of the Middle East."
In remarks that criticised the West, he said that certain unnamed forces were seeking to provoke further escalation and to draw as many other countries and peoples into the conflict as possible.
The aim, he said, was to "launch a real wave of chaos and mutual hatred not only in the Middle East but also far beyond its borders. For this purpose, among other things, they are trying to play on the national and religious feelings of millions of people."
Putin conveyed his condolences to the families of Israelis and citizens of other countries who were killed or wounded by Hamas in its bloody Oct. 7 attack.
Moscow, he said, continued to advocate for a two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli issue, something he said was the only way to reach a long-term settlement.
He made it clear though that he thought Israel was wrong to keep bombing Gaza in retaliation for the slaughter and hostage-taking of Israeli citizens by Hamas.
"It is also clear to us that innocent people should not be held responsible for crimes committed by others," said Putin.
"The fight against terrorism cannot be conducted according to the notorious principle of collective responsibility when old people, women, children, entire families and hundreds of thousands of people are left without shelter, food, water, electricity and medical care."
At least 24 journalist killed since Hamas attack on Oct 7 says journalist group
As of Wednesday, at least 24 journalists (20 Palestinian, 3 Israeli and 1 Lebanese) have been killed since the Hamas attack on October 7, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
An additional eight journalists were reported injured, while three journalists were reported missing or detained. The organization also flagged continued attacks, arrests, threats and censorship journalists are facing while covering the war.

TITLE: Hezbollah chief meets with Hamas, Islamic Jihad leaders in Lebanon, talk ways for 'real Gaza victory'
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-25T10:49:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2023-10-25/ty-article/hezbollah-chief-meets-with-hamas-islamic-jihad-leaders-in-lebanon-talk-gaza-victory/0000018b-65ac-d288-afef-f5fc701d0000

Hezbollah chief Hassan Nassrallah met with the head of Palestinian Islamic Jihad Ziad Nahleh and deputy head of Hamas' political bureau Saleh al-Arouri, according to a report by Hezbollah's al-Manar TV.
According to a Hezbollah statement, the three discussed the latest events in the Gaza Strip including the ongoing clashes on Lebanon's border with Israel. It was agreed to continue coordination and regular monitoring of developments on a daily and regular basis, the statement added.
It was also reported that they discussed the manner in which the "axis of resistance" should act in order to achieve a "real victory" in Gaza. In a photograph circulated from the meeting, the three are seen sitting while on the wall hang the pictures of the supreme leader of Iran, Ali Khamenei, and of the spiritual father of the Islamic Republic, Ayatollah Khomeini.
Since Hamas' attack on October 7, Hezbollah and IDF forces clashed and exchanged fire frequently along the Lebanese border. As a result, six IDF soldiers and a civilian were killed. According to Hezbollah, so far 40 of its members have been killed as a result of IDF attacks.
In recent days, the IDF said it had attacked several terrorist squads that were responsible for firing mortar bombs and anti-tank missiles at IDF forces and outposts. In addition, the Israeli Air Force attacked Hezbollah targets in Lebanon in response to missile fire towards Israel.
On Tuesday, the IDF attacked Syrian army targets in Daraa in the south of the country after two rockets were fired at Israeli locales in the Golan Heights. According to the IDF spokesperson, the army attacked military infrastructure and mortar bomb launchpads. The state media in Syria announced this morning that eight soldiers were killed in the Israeli strikes.

TITLE: The future of Medicine: Treatment for Diseases with Alpaca Antibodies
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-25T15:04:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/haaretz-labels/medica/2023-10-25/ty-article-labels/.premium/the-future-of-medicine-treatment-for-diseases-with-alpaca-antibodies/0000018b-66a1-de34-a1ef-7fe9dbcd0000

Monoclonal antibodies are considered to be in the forefront of the biotechnology industry in treating immunological diseases, especially cancer, because they are highly target-specific and clinically effective. However, antibody therapy comes with considerable side effects, which is an accepted risk in cancer treatment but limits the use of this therapy for chronic autoimmune diseases like psoriasis and severe asthma due to benefit-risk considerations. As a result, many patients with autoimmune diseases classified as mild to moderate have no access to biologic drugs and must settle for steroid-based treatments. These drugs lose their effectiveness with sustained use and come with long-term risks.
Scinai, a biopharmaceutical company specializing in innovative biological products for autoimmune and infectious disease treatment, maintains it has found a solution by using nano-antibodies produced from alpacas (nanoAbs). Amir Reichman, the company’s CEO, talks about the patented technology that they have developed.
The Connection Between Psoriasis and Alpacas
Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease that causes rashes, itching, and flaking. In addition to its non-aesthetic appearance, it can also lead to considerable pain and discomfort. According to Reichman, the solutions currently available do not provide a satisfactory response, primarily due to their side effects. He explains, "Current biologic drugs require the injection of antibodies that enter the bloodstream, spread throughout the body, and cause a wide range of side effects, some of which can be severe, such as the development of Crohn's disease. Today, biologic drugs are approved for use in approximately 50% of psoriasis patients, but in reality, only about 25% of them are using these drugs, mainly those with severe psoriasis." He points out that there is currently no suitable biologic drug for mild psoriasis, and patients with moderate cases are reluctant to use them due to the risks. "On the other hand, alpaca nano-antibodies enable the production of a small antibody that can be injected directly into the affected areas and will break down when it enters the bloodstream, limiting its effect to the localized areas. This will prevent systemic side effects associated with injecting drugs into the bloodstream. We aim to create the 'Botox for psoriasis patients' that will be given to patients with mild to moderate conditions and enable localized treatment. The treatment will only be administered when psoriasis symptoms appear, without requiring injections every two weeks as with existing drugs. The Max Planck Research Institute in Germany, our scientific partner from whom we acquired the patent license, has an alpaca farm. Using simple blood tests, they can quickly produce large quantities of nano-antibody libraries, and we select the best antibodies for injecting the substance directly into the affected area without spreading to other parts of the body. Alpaca antibodies are ten times smaller than human antibodies and have excellent targeting capabilities, which allows the substance to penetrate better and degrade rapidly. The psoriasis drug project is currently at the pre-clinical trial stage, planned to be ready for marketing by 2028."
Can this technology be applied to the development of drugs for other diseases as well?
"Definitely! For instance, asthma is treated systematically through subcutaneous injection of antibodies. Just like in the case of psoriasis, apart from the high cost of the drug, its use is associated with a risk of serious side effects. Here, too, alpaca nano-antibodies can be administered directly to the target organ, in this case through an inhaler into the lungs, for a precise and effective treatment with significantly reduced risk of side effects."
"Infectious diseases can also benefit from the use of nano-antibodies from alpacas. During the COVID-19 pandemic, we led a feasibility study to demonstrate its potential via inhalation of the antibody we developed to treat patients who had contracted the virus. In collaboration with the Fraunhofer Society, a major research institute in Germany, we successfully treated hamsters infected with COVID-19 through the inhalation of nano-antibodies. Another branch of the trial provided evidence of the potential use of nano-antibodies as a preventive measure by administering the nano-antibodies through inhalation three hours before virus exposure. In essence, we created a COVID-19 “iron dome" for the hamsters’ lungs that prevented infection, which led the U.S. Department of Health to express interest in the drug's development."
A growth engine for new developments and innovations
Amir Reichman was originally appointed as the CEO of BiondVax Pharmaceuticals in 2021 after the company’s failure to develop a universal flu vaccine. Reichman came to the company from the management of GSK Vaccines in Belgium in order to head its reorganization. Under his leadership, they acquired licenses for the development and commercialization of new patents for nano-antibodies for the treatment of autoimmune and infectious diseases. The company name was changed to Scinai Immunotherapeutics.
Reichman explains that his central aim was to move beyond focusing on a single product: "The success rate in biotechnology projects at the pre-clinical stage is about 5%. Developing a product from the patent stage to market launch can cost a billion dollars and take up to a decade in the best-case scenario. Therefore, the idea that a company can be built around a single product, like what happens in the high-tech industry, is fundamentally flawed and has led to reduced investments in the sector and the so-called "ecosystem failure" in Israel. I transformed this paradigm into a business model for the company that focuses on a vision to bring the necessary technologies to create future products. We use the nano-antibodies platform to develop drugs for a wide range of diseases, such as psoriasis, asthma, cystic fibrosis, as well as infectious diseases like COVID-19 and influenza. In addition to the technology, the team and organizational processes are crucial. We’ve added to high-quality company content that is based on a promising technology platform that can generate various products, thus preventing the company's failure in case one product fails in clinical trials."
Research and Development Services Unit
In addition to its R&D unit, the company also operates a Contract Development and Manufacturing Organization (CDMO) unit that provides outsourced R&D services to other startups in the biotechnology field. These services are provided in a state-of-the-art facility in Jerusalem, capable of producing large quantities of products at the GMP level required for clinical trials in Israel, Europe, and the United States. Reichman aims to incorporate artificial intelligence to create antibody libraries artificially, which will preclude the need for alpacas and enable the development of even better drugs while saving time and money.
To the Scinai Immunotherapeutics website >>
Partnered with Scinai Immunotherapeutics

TITLE: Spy satellites over Syria reveal hundreds of ancient Roman forts
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-26T06:08:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/archaeology/2023-10-26/ty-article-magazine/spy-satellites-over-syria-reveal-hundreds-of-ancient-roman-forts/0000018b-624e-d288-afef-f2deff9e0000

Aviation goes back over 2,000 years if one counts kites, or to the 18th-century invention of the hot-air balloon if one insists that a person be involved in rising skyward. But by the 1920s airplanes were aloft, and it came to pass that the Jesuit archaeologist the Rev. Antoine Poidebard – a veteran pilot in World War I – flew over the Syrian steppe, pioneering the aerial survey of ancient ruins. He flew a biplane, explaining that due to the immense distances, it could hardly be done by motor car.
Flying over Syria, Iraq and Jordan between 1925 and 1932, Fr. Poidebard observed and photographed hundreds of ancient fortified compounds. He deduced what they were and published his findings in 1934: traces of Rome.
These were the ruins of fortresses protecting the Roman Empire’s eastern frontier, Poidebard postulated: a line of defense against incursions from the east.
And then came the Cold War, which began in 1947, followed by the invention of spy satellites. Many photographs were taken of the Syrian steppe over which Poidebard had flown, and beyond. The images from the CIA’s Corona and Hexagon programs have now been declassified; they show another 396 ancient Roman forts scattered through the northern Fertile Crescent. Some were in areas over which the Jesuit missionary had flown; others were in areas he hadn’t surveyed.
Writing in the journal of Antiquity, Jesse Casana of Dartmouth University and colleagues present some of the satellite images and a new theory for these ruins. Their dispersion and the vast distances between them belie Poidebard’s defensive frontier thesis. Their role was to facilitate the movement of peoples and goods in the region. Roman soldiers too, but a sort of defensive wall they were not.
This in turn suggests that Rome’s frontiers were – at least sometimes – places of “cultural exchange” rather than perennial war zones, the authors suggest.
Can’t go there
Either theory, Poidebard’s or the new one, is based on all these structures being from the same span of time, the Roman period. Poidebard believed they dated primarily to the second and third centuries, the late Roman period. But that thesis has always been contentious, Casana and the team say.
Near Easterners have been building fortifications for at least 6,000 years, if not before. Also, the construction of fortifications didn’t end with the Romans. Yet Casana and the team did ultimately agree, based on evidence from recent excavations and surveys, that most of the forts discussed by their article do date to the second to sixth centuries.
A small proportion are earlier and some are later, but they do think most were Roman – while noting the difficulty in dating more reliably based on meticulous excavation of hundreds of sites over vast areas that are not exactly accessible.
Not to mention, they add, “excavations at numerous Roman-period fort sites have recovered few diagnostic artifacts,” and sites can be littered with artifacts from later occupation.
But they agree there were hundreds and hundreds of Roman forts. Poidebard aloft in his rinky-dink biplane thought they ran between north and south along the eastern boundary of the empire. But the bigger picture, augmented by the spy satellite images, paints an east-west line following the northern edge of the great Arabian desert, connecting Mosul on the mighty River Tigris in the east with Syria’s Aleppo in the west.
Poidebard had actually set off specifically to find evidence of Roman fortifications along the empire’s eastern frontier, which history tells us had been heavily fortified by the emperors Septimius Severus (who served from 193-201) and Diocletian (284-305), Casana and the team explain.
But the aviating father actually followed a road, the Strata Diocletiana, the emperor had built, thereby opening the door to discovery bias. Indeed, he observed hundreds of fortified buildings, which he photographed from the air. Some he visited on foot as well, including Syria’s Tell Brak – a settlement that goes back at least 7,000 years.
Anyway, he thusly concluded that the forts dated to the Roman time and protected its frontier against Arab and Persian invaders. His colleagues at the time applauded roundly but some did point out snags to the theory – a key one being that the forts seemed to be too distant from one another to function as a line of defense.
A tweak on the thesis, delivered decades later, was that the forts protected "strategic oases" for armies and trade caravans. Or that they protected local communities against marauders – quadruped-propelled banditry is nothing new, and nor is abduction for ransom.
Underneath the chickpeas
Theories abounded over the decades, but proof on the ground remained scanty because there has been very little excavation of these fortifications.
Note that the giant Roman army camp discovered at Legio, by Tell Megiddo in Israel, is the only Roman army camp to be found in the empire’s east. Jerusalem is also supposed to have been home to a huge legionnaires’ army camp, but that has never been found. These fortifications described in the article aren’t army camps per se, but the Romans did like to follow certain rules, it seems, whether building army bases or just forts.
“The most common form that we interpret as a probable fort is a classic square shape, typically 50-80 meters [about 165-260 feet] per side,” the authors explain. These buildings are usually isolated, not part of a settlement and are often located in “marginal environments,” nowhere near other evidence of settlement (ancient or modern).
The most important observation is the spatial distribution of the forts and fort-like archaeological finds, they sum up.
So, Poidebard’s forts were concentrated along the route of what he figured was Rome’s eastern frontier, following Diocletian’s road. Hence the discovery bias: he flew where he thought they were, but he didn’t look elsewhere. The spy satellite imagery shows the forts spread over a vast region, spanning from east to west at the edge of the desert, with a “remarkably dense” concentration of forts in the bleak western Jazireh – an area unblessed with notable surface water, at least since the last time Arabia was green.
They also note that their work may suffer from preservation bias: many of these structures may have disappeared from the archaeological record entirely, especially in relatively densely occupied or cultivated areas. Note that the vast Roman camp at Legio in Israel is covered by Kibbutz Megiddo’s chickpea fields.
In fact, the more they analyzed the images, the more forts (or fort-like structures) they found.
So what have we? Remote sensing resulting in the discovery and mapping of 396 previously unrecognized Roman ruins throughout the desert margins of eastern Syria and northwestern Iraq, compared with the 116 that the Jesuit pilot had noticed in those parts. Most are Roman, the researchers deduce.
Some remained in use through to the medieval period, they add – but most, certainly the smaller ones, were abandoned by the sixth century – but they couldn’t have served as some sort of defensive wall for the Roman Empire against invaders. Their real role was more likely to help caravans cross the bandit-beset drylands, essentially serving as sites for cultural exchanges: “Offering water to camels and livestock, and providing a place for weary travelers to eat, drink and sleep, thereby playing a critical role in bringing east and west together.” For a while at least.

TITLE: "We are proud that our growth creates jobs in Israel’s periphery"
SOURCE: haaretz
DATE: 2023-10-26T10:16:00+03:00
URL: https://www.haaretz.com/haaretz-labels/2023-10-26/ty-article-labels/.premium/we-are-proud-that-our-growth-creates-jobs-in-israels-periphery/0000018b-6ac0-d979-a3bb-ebf718160000

Resonetics has positioned itself in recent years as a leading player in the field of developing and manufacturing medical devices. The company specializes in advanced technological solutions and provides engineering, prototyping, development and production services for start-ups and various companies in the medical technology industry (MedTech). Throughout its years of activity, Resonetics has helped develop a long line of cutting-edge medical devices in its centers around the world, including the Israeli factory located in Or Akiva.
"Our mission is to lead on a global level in aspects of engineering, prototyping, product development and micro-manufacturing of medical technologies," says Matthew Robida, Senior Vice President of Resonetics. "The basic aim of Resonetics is to bring about a positive change in the lives of patients, so our work is directed to developing products that will achieve this goal worldwide. We want companies to be able to turn to us for assistance when they need to quickly develop new and innovative medical devices, and when they need a reliable manufacturing partner. Resonetics invests substantial resources in developing focused production capabilities and in establishing technical expertise so that we can solve complex production problems and produce the parts that no other company can solve or 
produce."
What does the company’s portfolio of solutions and services look like?
"Resonetics focuses mainly on helping medical technology companies at the beginning of a new project – building prototypes and product development, and later on producing components, assemblies and finished products. We have invested heavily in a network of Lightspeed Labs with dedicated resources for rapidly producing prototypes and process development. Each of the laboratories has technological expertise and is located in one of the main hubs of the MedTech industry. Our staff knows how to assist customers at every stage of product development – from basic concept development to mass production.
"After the products developed in a Lightspeed Lab are ready for commercial launch, we have a standard process for transferring production to a team that specializes in this. Thanks to our substantial resources in both personnel and equipment, we are able to increase our production scale to meet customer demands. In addition, Resonetics has diversified its production solutions for processing metals and polymers."
Direct communication between engineers
So why do companies decide to outsource their development processes in partnership with Resonetics instead of doing the development work independently? "Different types of companies come to us for different reasons," answers Robida. "When it comes to large companies, we can offer speed and flexibility to the development process, which is not always easy for them to do in-house. In addition, we can expand the capabilities of their in-house staff or bring focused expertise related to a certain type of device. For young startups, or companies with smaller staffs, we can fully manage the product development process. Our product development team collaborates with companies at all stages of the development lifecycle, so we can help different projects where they are needed.
"We have an experienced team of more than 50 engineers with focused expertise in the area of interventional devices, especially related to structural heart, cryotherapy, and various vascular applications," he adds. "We strive to cooperate with our customers, which is why we prioritize direct communication between engineers and open dialogue.
"For companies looking to quickly produce different designs for a product, we offer a Lightspeed Lab day where customers can come to our factory for a joint development experience. They benefit from an engineer at their disposal, a production technician and equipment that can produce a range of designs throughout the day."
In what ways does Resonetics help its customers with production solutions?
"Our goal is always to develop a repeatable process, which can quickly lead to production. When we have customers with a new product, the engineers from the Lightspeed Lab spend time reviewing the drawings and conduct an open dialogue with them regarding the design’s impact on future production. During the development process, our team knows that the ultimate goal is commercial production, and therefore we place the highest priority on reliable processes that can be replicated on a large scale."
How does the company maintain its leading position with regard to new technologies?
"Technological leadership is at the core of our business and we treat speed and innovation as basic principles in our operational culture. We have a group that is made up of technological experts in various fields, whose goal is to accelerate our in-house research and development ventures. We invest in improving our existing capabilities and developing completely new ones. We also have an in-house instrumentation and automation team that designs and builds customized equipment according to our needs, and this allows us to develop new production processes and advance existing processes. Resonetics also focuses on investing resources in automation in order to create dependable and efficient production processes, which will provide our customers with reliable components with consistent production quality. Our Israeli factory recently received several investments in the field of automation, including in advanced test equipment."
Unique processing capabilities
Resonetics’ factory in Israel provides solutions for laser cutting, laser welding, thermal treatments, surface treatments, assembly in a clean environment and braiding. "We assist with the customers' products, from the construction of prototypes to production, including the assembly of finished products in a clean room environment," says Daniel Hazanov, Vice President of Operations at Resonetics Israel. "Our staff has extensive experience in cutting various metals and alloys such as nitinol, cobalt-chromium, stainless steel and titanium. We manufacture components for a wide range of medical uses, such as neurological diseases, heart diseases and ophthalmology. Here too we offer construction of prototypes and production mass, in accordance with ISO standards and FDA license requirements."
Hazanov explains Resonetics’ decision to invest in Israel in terms of the innovation capabilities that are available in the country. "The ecosystem in Israel is very innovative and has led to the creation of some of the best-selling medical devices in the industry. Israelis enjoy a reputation for strong personalities and an affinity for innovation. The nitinol processing capabilities in our factory were also a significant factor in the decision to invest in Israel. Nitinol is a critical raw material in the medical products industry and it's not easy to work with. The team here has developed some unique processing capabilities based on the requirements of the medical startup community in Israel."
Is there synergy between your capabilities and Resonetics’ other centers?
"Yes. For example, we can cut a nitinol frame for a medical device, which is then covered with polymer and undergoes laser drilling at the Resonetics plant in New Hampshire, USA."
Improving processing capabilities
The company's presence in Israel began with the purchase of STI Laser Industries in 2018. This was a strategic step for Resonetics, after it recognized Israeli innovation in everything related to the medical device industry and worked to establish a factory in Israel that could support the local industry. "STI Laser was the right choice because it enjoyed an excellent reputation when it comes to working with companies in laser cutting of nitinol and cobalt chromium components, especially for uses in the treatment of heart disease and neurological diseases," explains Hazanov. "Since then, Resonetics has also invested in another Israeli company called Medibrane, which has developed innovative technology for polymer coating and coverings of medical devices. Like STI Laser, Medibrane is also very development-oriented and supports the medical technology industry in Israel and around the world."
The Resonetics factory in Israel is located in Or Akiva, in an area that is not necessarily considered a center of innovation and technology. How does this location affect the company's activity?
"We are proud that our factory is located in Israel’s periphery and that our growth creates new jobs in the region. The founder of STI Laser, Tobi Sivan, chose Or Akiva specifically to create more jobs in areas that are relatively far from the center and economically weak. Our staff work extremely hard and take our activity very seriously. Our products are intended for critical medical devices and our customers rely on them. We greatly value our staff and want to provide them with the safe and positive environment in which they can succeed."
What about the future? What are the plans for the continued operation of the Israeli factory?
"The factory has a very promising future. We are developing several medical devices with strategic customers that will have a significant impact on the industry and the expansion of the Israeli factory. We have invested heavily in the factory's infrastructure and we are ready to take on additional projects, which will allow us to create more jobs in the region."
How does Resonetics see its future in Israel?
Robida: "Resonetics is committed to continuing to invest in its operations in Israel. Since our original purchase of the plant in Israel, we have expanded both in size and in our processing capabilities. We built a second building in 2020 to support our continued growth and have nearly doubled our workforce. In addition, we are improving our processing capabilities by adding new and advanced equipment, including automated electropolishing and fast laser processing machines, specially designed and built by the company's equipment team. We have also enlarged our clean rooms to meet the demand for product assembly in the variety of our programs related to the next generation of medical products, which are expected to generate significant growth in the coming years. We are happy to continue creating jobs in Israel while supporting the needs of the vibrant, local and international MedTech industry."
Increased consolidation in the medical industry
"The world of MedTech has changed significantly in recent years, especially following the global pandemic" says Matthew Robida. "As elective medical procedures were halted, the result was a short-term drop in demand for related devices. And later, when demand recovered, it brought with it challenges along the entire supply chain. Recently, there has been increased consolidation in the industry, with larger companies acquiring innovative companies and technologies with the aim of expanding their range of products. Regulatory requirements became more stringent, which lengthened the schedules and increased the costs of obtaining regulatory approval. This change made it difficult for start-ups to succeed and thus accelerated the consolidation."
In collaboration with Resonetics
